meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The review is mixed: one week accept and two week reject. The concerns are serious but fixable. Points to address: Annotation quality dataset/statistics details dataset vs method contribution | The paper is strong as a dataset, atlas, and application/resource paper rather than as a novel segmentation-method paper. The methodological pipeline appears to rely largely on existing components, but the expert annotation effort, multiscale integration, and cell-type-specific hippocampal density mapping are potentially useful to the community. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The final revised recommendations are two Accepts (R1, R3) and one Reject (R2). However, it is worth noting that R2 changed their recommendation from Weak Accept to Reject after seeing the earlier recommendations from the other reviewers, both of whom later changed their recommendations to Accept. All reviewers believe that the paper can be further improved for the camera-ready version without significant additional work. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a multiscale pipeline for reconstructing cell-type-resolved neuronal density maps in the human hippocampus from BigBrain histology. Its main contributions are an expert-validated three-class hippocampal cell annotation dataset, a human-in-the-loop annotation/segmentation pipeline, a compact density estimation model in the 20 µm BigBrain space, and a 3D point-cloud reconstruction of excitatory, inhibitory, and glial cell distributions across the CA complex. The initial reviews were mixed and overall borderline, with scores of 3 / 4 / 3.Reviewers appreciated the potential value of the work as a resource contribution, especially the expert-validated hippocampal cell dataset and the possibility of producing cell-type-specific density maps at scale. However, the reviewers raised several concerns: limited methodological novelty, unclear positioning of the contribution as a dataset/resource versus a new method, insufficient details on dataset construction and registration, uncertainty about annotation quality and inter-annotator variability, limited instance-level segmentation analysis, and questions about the biological interpretation of the reported CA-wise cell counts. The rebuttal addressed several of these concerns. The authors clarified that the main contribution should be understood primarily as an expert-validated dataset/resource and mesoscopic atlas, rather than as a purely methodological advance. They provided additional information on annotation quality, including inter- and intra-expert AER, the final AER being within expert variability, and the fact that annotations were expert-reviewed. They also clarified the motivation for the adaptive thresholding module, the HR-to-LR transfer strategy, the construction of matched HR/LR data, and the biological interpretation of the CA-wise counts by comparing neuron-like counts with prior estimates. Some concerns remain. In particular, the final manuscript should more clearly describe the implementation and contribution of the ATM component, class-wise annotation reliability, the role of merged models, registration details, and the consistency of the matched HR/LR data. The ablation of ATM versus the full merged pipeline remains incomplete, and the biological interpretation should still be carefully framed as an atlas/resource contribution rather than a fully validated biological conclusion. After rebuttal, the reviewer opinions are A / R / A. Reviewers 1 and 3 moved from weak reject to accept, mainly because the rebuttal clarified the contribution, provided annotation-quality evidence, and better grounded the biological interpretation. Reviewer 2 moved to reject, emphasizing that some methodological details and design choices remain insufficiently justified. I place greater weight on the two positive post-rebuttal assessments and on the value of the dataset/resource contribution, while acknowledging that the methodology itself is not the primary strength. I recommend Accept. The paper is not a strong methodological contribution, but it provides a useful and difficult-to-obtain resource for the community, and the rebuttal sufficiently mitigated the most serious concerns regarding annotation quality and contribution framing. The remaining issues should be addressed in the camera-ready version, especially the clarification of ATM, merged-model details, annotation reliability, and the interpretation of the density maps.

title: CerviThink: A Reinforced Visual Reasoning Framework for Cervical Cancer Cell Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper involves a substantial amount of work. The authors do not only propose a training framework, but also build a task-specific dataset, CerviCoT, to support the reasoning process in cervical cell classification. Another strength is that the paper introduces several task-motivated modifications that are reasonable for this problem setting. The grounding-answering decomposition, the focus/transform/ignore operations, and the DVHR design are all aligned with the intuition of how difficult cytology cases may need to be examined more carefully.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper does not sufficiently establish that the RAG-generated rationales truly reflect pathologists’ diagnostic reasoning. CerviCoT is constructed by retrieving PubMed literature and generating step-by-step CoT rationales. This may be useful as weak supervision, and the ablation suggests it improves performance. However, the paper does not provide clinician verification, faithfulness assessment, or any expert agreement analysis showing that these rationales actually reconstruct how pathologists reason in practice. At present, the paper demonstrates utility of synthetic rationales, but not their fidelity to real diagnostic reasoning. 2.The methodological novelty appears moderate relative to the underlying Ground-R1/GRPO paradigm. The paper clearly adapts ideas from Ground-R1, including grounded visual reasoning and RL-based optimization, and builds on Qwen2.5-VL with a task-specific pipeline. In my view, the main novelty lies in the domain adaptation, the ignore operation in the cytology setting, the CerviCoT dataset, and the DVHR design. These are potentially useful contributions, but the core algorithmic backbone remains close to existing grounded RL reasoning frameworks. As a result, the novelty is more incremental/task-specialized than fundamentally methodological. 3.Strong vision-only baselines are missing. The empirical comparison is largely against LVLM-family baselines. For this task, especially once the input has already been cropped into 256×256 cell regions, strong pure-vision baselines such as ComparisonDetector, ResNet/ViT patch classifiers, or MIL/detection-first pipelines would be highly relevant and likely competitive. Their absence makes it difficult to judge whether the reported gains reflect a real advance over established cytology pipelines, or mainly an improvement within the LVLM comparison set. 4.There are reproducibility and reporting gaps. Important details are missing or under-specified, including reward weighting rationale, transform/inpainting parameterization, training stability measures, few-shot protocol details, and the exact role of bounding boxes. The paper also states that no explicit bounding box annotations are required, yet bounding boxes appear to be used for data construction and cropping. This distinction should be clarified more carefully.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.This paper addresses a clinically meaningful and challenging task. Cervical cell classification is strongly affected by subtle morphological differences, cell overlap, and imaging artifacts. The authors focus on the limitations of existing CAD systems and general LVLMs in complex scenarios, particularly their insufficient performance and limited interpretability. The problem setting itself therefore has clear practical value. 2.The overall methodological idea is relatively novel and well motivated. Rather than treating the task as a standard image classification problem, the paper attempts to mimic the diagnostic workflow of pathologists by decoupling “localizing critical regions” from “making classification decisions,” thereby building a reasoning framework that is better aligned with the clinical analysis process. This grounding-answering design fits the nature of the task well. The design of the dynamic visual operations is insightful. In particular, the ignore operation is not merely used to mask out regions, but instead masks suspicious abnormal cells and examines whether the remaining background is normal, thereby simulating a degree of differential diagnostic reasoning. This design makes the method more tailored to medical scenarios than generic visual reasoning frameworks. 3.The experimental section reports not only the main results but also includes a certain level of ablation analysis. According to the paper, CerviThink achieves an F1-score of 74.80 on the DST dataset, outperforming multiple general-purpose and pathology-related baselines. In the few-shot settings on ComparisonDetector and HiCervix, it also shows clear improvements over the SFT and RL variants. The ablations on CerviCoT and the reward components further support the effectiveness of both the data construction strategy and the full DVHR mechanism.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The overall framework is clearly inspired by existing grounded visual reasoning and RL-based LVLM methods, especially works closely related to Ground-R1 [1]. In the current manuscript, the main incremental contributions appear to lie primarily in the cervical cell-specific data construction, the ignore operation, and the DVHR design. However, the paper does not yet sufficiently clarify whether these modifications constitute substantive methodological innovations or are mainly task-specific engineering adaptations. 2.The important experimental details remain unclear, including the class distribution of the DST dataset, whether the train/test split is performed at the patient level, the exact sampling protocol for the few-shot setting, whether the experiments were repeated across multiple random seeds, and the key hyperparameters used in reinforcement learning training. The current implementation details are too brief to support reproducibility. 3.The main tables report only single-run Precision, Recall, and F1-score, without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or statistical significance analysis. Given that this is a medical image classification task and may involve class imbalance, reporting only weighted F1 is not sufficient. Providing per-class results, a confusion matrix, and more clinically relevant metrics would better support the paper’s conclusions. 4.The paper’s claims regarding “interpretability” and “human-like reasoning” are stronger than the evidence currently provided. Although the method introduces structured outputs such as , , and , and designs a visual reasoning pipeline, there is still insufficient qualitative analysis showing whether the model has truly learned clinically meaningful reasoning processes. For instance, the paper does not show whether the localized regions align with the areas of interest used by pathology experts, nor does it include failure case analysis or expert evaluation to support the claim of improved interpretability. A case study would be more appropriate. 5.Some of the assumptions behind the reward design may be overly strong, especially the background normality confirmation reward, which assumes that after masking the suspected abnormal cells, the remaining region should be classified as normal. In real pathological images, however, multiple abnormal regions may coexist, or the surrounding background itself may contain diagnostically relevant abnormal cues. Therefore, this assumption may not always hold. The paper does not sufficiently discuss the applicability range or potential limitations of this design. [1] Cao, M., Zhao, H., Zhang, C., Chang, X., Reid, I., & Liang, X. (2025). Ground-r1: Incentivizing grounded visual reasoning via reinforcement learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.20272.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their insightful feedback. We address key concerns below: 1.Methodological Novelty vs. Ground-R1 (R1, R2) We respectfully clarify that CerviThink transitions from the passive spatial grounding of Ground-R1 to active sequential reasoning. Ground-R1’s static extractive cropping is insufficient for cytology, where dense overlapping demands hypothesis-driven deduction. We advance this in three ways: (1) Instead of merely locating a cell, we structurally redefine the action space using an Ignore operation to actively intervene in the visual state. By masking the suspected lesion, it forces the model to decouple the foreground and verify the local background morphology, simulating a clinical “rule-out” process absent in Ground-R1.(2) To handle micro-textures, our Transform operation utilizes dynamic zooming and contrast adjustments. This actively resolves fine-grained features like chromatin details that remain inherently ambiguous at Ground-R1’s global scale. (3) Finally, our DVHR shifts the optimization target from standard spatial grounding to enforcing logical consistency across these visual interventions. This ensures all reasoning steps conceptually align, overcoming the limitations of conventional models in complex cytopathological scenes. 2.Clinical Validation & Interpretability (R1, R2) During the development of CerviCoT dataset, we collaborated with pathologists to review the generated reasoning paths. Their assessment confirmed that the model’s outputs exhibit clinical fidelity and align with the Bethesda system workflows. 3.Missing Vision-Only Baselines (R1) During our comprehensive baseline evaluations, we assessed vision-only models on the DST dataset. Specifically, ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 achieved F1-scores of 68.12% and 71.85%, respectively, compared to CerviThink’s 74.80% on the DST Dataset. Unlike vision-only models that overfit to background artifacts and struggle with borderline cases, our sequential interventions effectively isolate and verify morphological features. 4.Assumption on Background Normality (R2) We agree with this insightful observation. In scenarios with multiple lesions, masking a single cell does not guarantee a completely normal background. Currently, this reward functions as a soft regularizer that encourages local context verification, thereby preventing the model from relying solely on the most salient lesion. We will explicitly discuss this assumption as a limitation in the revision and outline our future work on multi-instance masking strategies for complex, multi-lesion samples. 5.Reproducibility & Hyperparameters (R1, R2) To prevent data leakage, the 4:1 train/test and few-shot splits were performed strictly at the patient level. We will update all tables with standard deviations and per-class metrics. Regarding the role of bounding boxes, explicit annotations were used solely for initial data preprocessing. During RL training and inference, while the model dynamically generates spatial coordinates to guide visual operations, these coordinates are never supervised by ground-truth bounding boxes. Instead, spatial localization is driven entirely by the downstream reasoning rewards. For the hyperparameters, we set G1=4 and G2=2.KL divergence constraints were excluded, the clipping range was set to ε=0.2, and all DVHR components were weighted equally (1.0). Exact transform and inpainting parameterizations will also be fully detailed in the revision. 6.Figures & Formatting (R3) We will redesign Figure 1 to explicitly illustrate the tensor data flow, including inputs, policy network routing, and dynamic visual operations. All table captions will be moved to the top per conference guidelines.

title: Clinical-Injection Transformer with Domain-Adapted MAE for Lupus Nephritis Prognosis Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: The topic is clinically relevant and fits the general scope of MICCAI, and the authors attempt multimodal fusion and validation on a standard clinical dataset.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: [1] lack of novelty: The proposed framework is a simple combination of existing modules (e. g. , attention, fusion, generative augmentation) without novel designs, new theoretical insights, or specialized mechanisms for medical data. [2] The technical pipeline is ad-hoc and lacks clear motivation. Key designs (e. g. , attention mechanism, feature fusion, generative module) are not well justified or tailored to the clinical task. [3] The writing is unclear, notations are inconsistent, figures are not well-explained, and some technical descriptions are ambiguous or incomplete.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Pediatric lupus nephritis prognosis prediction from biopsy images appears substantially underexplored and the paper focuses on a clinically meaningful response task. The method uses routine PAS-stained pathology plus structured clinical variables which is more practical and potentially lower-cost. The Clinical-Injection Transformer is a clean, parameter-efficient fusion strategy that places clinical and image tokens in a shared self-attention space rather than relying on other heavier dual-stream fusion. The paper also reports the fusion block is lightweight with around 0.56M parameters. The decoupled knowledge adaptation and the multi-granularity morphology injection are well motivated and fit the pathology setting well. The method improves over image-only MIL baselines, a clinical-only MLP, late fusion, and cross-attention fusion, with especially notable gains in macro-F1 for minority classes. The paper separately studies fusion architecture, feature extractor choice, and morphology type injection, which strengthens the technical case. Generally clear presentation. The framework overview, module definitions, and training setup are presented clearly enough for the overall method to be understandable.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper does not clearly specify how the 5-class morphology classifier used for type injection was trained relative to the downstream 5-fold CV on the 71 patient prognosis cohort. If morphology predictions for a test fold were generated by a model trained on those patients, that would inflate performance. This should be clarified explicitly. The 0m+3m setting includes “treatment response features”, but the exact variables are not described clearly enough to assess how directly they overlap with the 12-month endpoint definition. This matters for interpreting the clinical forecasting claim.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1) Existing histopathology-based methods for LN require four costly staining protocols and do not incorporate clinical data. This work represents the first multimodal framework that performs three-class prediction using only routine PAS-stained biopsy images and structured clinical data, demonstrating strong potential for clinical translation. 2) To address the issue that fine-tuning models directly for morphological classification discards subtle texture features useful for prognosis, the authors froze the MAE-pretrained backbone for feature extraction, and injected morphological classification results via one-hot vectors and distribution vectors. Ablation studies confirmed the benefit of this design. 3) To mitigate the small dataset problem, this work projects clinical features into a condition token, which is fed into a shallow 2-layer Transformer together with image patch tokens. This reduces the number of parameters and lowers the risk of overfitting.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: It is not specified whether patches from patients in the test fold were excluded from the pretraining corpus for each fold in the 5-fold cross-validation. Without strict patient-level isolation, the model may have seen test data during pretraining, which could lead to inflated performance estimates. The study data were collected from only 71 patients at a single hospital, with no external multi-center independent validation set. Therefore, the model’s generalization ability across different institutions, staining batches, scanning devices, and patient populations cannot be verified. It is not clarified whether MICE imputation was performed uniformly on the entire dataset, or strictly fitted on the training set and then applied to the test set within cross-validation. The former would constitute data leakage. In the introduction, the authors mentioned mainstream multimodal fusion methods in pathology and claimed that they are prone to overfitting. However, the comparative experiments only include single-modal MIL, simple late fusion, and the cross-attention module of MCAT, without comparison against full end-to-end state-of-the-art multimodal pathology models. At least one complete SOTA multimodal pathology baseline should be added to numerically demonstrate the advantages of the proposed CIT module under small-sample conditions.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers and the Area Chair for their careful feedback. We address each concern below. 1.Cross-Validation Protocol (Reviewer #2, Reviewer #3, Meta-Reviewer #2) Morphology Classifier (Reviewer #2). The type labels injected downstream (Sec. 2.4) are the discrete predictions of the fine-tuned classifier described in Sec. 2.2.For each CV fold, this classifier is retrained on the training and validation splits; its predictions on the held-out test patients are used as the type labels, ensuring no information transfer across folds. MICE Imputation (Reviewer #3). MICE is applied exclusively to pre-outcome clinical features (0-month and 3-month), strictly excluding outcome labels. Crucially, to prevent feature leakage, imputation is performed independently within each cross-validation fold. The imputer is fitted solely on the training split and transforms the unseen validation/test splits, ensuring no prospective or cross-sample leakage occurs. 2.Clinical Feature Specification (Reviewer #2) The 59 features (3 demographics, 22 baseline, 17 three-month, 17 deltas) span urinalysis, blood routine, renal biochemistry, immunological markers (C3, C4, ANA, anti-dsDNA), anthropometrics, and disease activity (SLEDAI-2K). The 3-month features and deltas capture early treatment response and are temporally distinct from the 12-month outcome. A more detailed specification will be provided in the camera-ready version. 3.Methodological Novelty (Reviewer #1) CIT introduces a novel cross-modal paradigm. Existing multimodal pathology methods either use separate cross-attention modules (MCAT) that overfit on small cohorts, or channel-wise modulation (FiLM, DAFT) that applies the same transformation to all patches without spatial selectivity. CIT places clinical features as a condition token within the same self-attention sequence as image patches, so every patch can attend to clinical context and the clinical token can attend to relevant patches—all within a single module. This unified attention space is a structurally different approach to multimodal interaction. The decoupled MAE addresses a limitation of standard fine-tuning: fine-tuning on an auxiliary diagnostic task narrows representations and discards prognostic features (yielding a +6.0% Acc improvement over standard fine-tuning, Table 2b). Our decoupling—frozen MAE for self-supervised features, discrete labels for morphological knowledge—preserves both. Multi-granularity type injection exploits the hierarchical nature of pathological assessment. Patch-level one-hot encoding constrains which instances the model attends to, while patient-level type distribution provides global lesion context to the clinical token (+2.3% Acc, +5.5% M-F1, Table 2c). 4.Ethics Statement (Reviewer #2, Meta-Reviewer #2) We appreciate this important reminder. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Guangzhou Women and Children’s Medical Center. We will include an explicit ethics statement in the camera-ready version. 5.Single-Center Limitation (Reviewer #3) We agree with this assessment and have acknowledged it in Sec. 4.The 71-patient cohort reflects the inherent rarity of pediatric LN (childhood-onset SLE incidence: 0.3–0.9 per 100,000 child-years); even the largest multicenter biopsy-confirmed pediatric LN studies report ~300 patients [Chan et al., KI Reports, 2023]. We are actively pursuing multi-center collaboration to extend this work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): I recommend a Provisional Accept because the paper addresses a significant, underexplored clinical need in pediatric lupus nephritis prognosis. It introduces a parameter-efficient Clinical-Injection Transformer (CIT) containing approximately 0.56M parameters, which effectively mitigates the risk of overfitting on small datasets. The framework demonstrates strong quantitative performance by achieving 90.1% accuracy and 89.4% AUC, showing clear improvements over single-modality baselines. While Reviewer 1 raised concerns regarding a lack of novelty and an ad-hoc pipeline , the authors’ use of decoupled MAE knowledge adaptation is well-motivated for preserving prognostically relevant features in this specific pathology context. Reviewers 2 and 3 questioned the evaluation protocol and the limitations of a small, single-center dataset ; however, this cohort size is consistent with the field given the rarity of childhood-onset SLE and the difficulty of acquiring digitized longitudinal biopsy data. For the camera-ready version, the authors must explicitly detail their cross-validation protocol to ensure no data leakage occurred during MICE imputation and morphology classifier training , and they must include a clear statement confirming ethics and IRB approval for the clinical data.

title: Collaborative Topology and Connectivity Learning for EM Neuron Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Proposed a two-stage collaborative framework that incorporates neuron skeletons and distance transform maps as explicit prior knowledge, effectively resolving split and merge errors caused by ambiguous boundaries and complex topologies in EM images. 2.Designed the ACWM module to stabilize multi-task feature extraction, and utilized the BRR module for intelligent feature routing, fundamentally preventing the negative transfer issue prevalent in traditional multi-task learning.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Abrupt Introduction and Insufficient Justification of the Pruning Module: The primary narrative of the paper focuses on addressing the pain point of “improving neuron topology and connectivity accuracy. “ Therefore, the sudden introduction of the “Gradient-based Structural Filter Pruning” module appears abrupt and somewhat disconnected from the core motivation. If the goal of this pruning is to handle latency constraints in large-scale applications, Table 4 should report the actual inference time required per 3D block. Reductions in parameter count and FLOPs do not inherently guarantee faster practical inference speeds. Furthermore, the authors should provide a direct comparison of inference latency against other baseline methods to convincingly demonstrate the true effectiveness of this pruning module. 2.Hidden Overhead of Auxiliary Label Generation: The proposed network relies heavily on the “skeleton” and “distance transform map” as auxiliary supervision signals. However, in real-world, ultra-large-scale EM connectomics research, computing 3D skeletons offline is an exceptionally time-consuming process. The authors should explicitly report the time overhead required for generating these labels and critically discuss whether this dependency limits the scalability of the proposed method for massive neuron segmentation tasks. 3.Training Overhead of the Multi-Task Architecture: While the designs of the ACWM and BRR mechanisms are highly ingenious, does the simultaneous prediction of three targets (affinity, skeleton, and distance map) significantly inflate the computational overhead and GPU memory consumption during the training phase? 4.Discrepancy Regarding Parameter Counts (Table 4 vs. Fig. 1): I noticed a significant discrepancy regarding the model size. According to Table 4, the parameter count for “Stage 1” is exactly identical to that of “Stage 2”. However, as illustrated in the architecture diagram (Fig. 1), Stage 2 incorporates an additional BRR module and subsequent refinement steps compared to Stage 1.Logically, adding these extra fusion and refinement modules should increase the total number of trainable parameters. Could the authors explain this inconsistency? 5.Ambiguity in Experimental Evaluation Protocols (Tables 1 & 4): There is considerable ambiguity regarding the evaluation settings presented in Tables 1 and 4.Based on the proposed architecture, my understanding is that Stage 2 sequentially depends on Stage 1.However, the descriptions and formatting in the tables make it appear as though Stage 1 and Stage 2 were separated and evaluated completely independently. The authors must explicitly clarify this evaluation protocol to prevent reader confusion and ensure reproducibility.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The explicit split of two stages and introduction of meaningful long-range/local shape priors seems quite novel and useful. Neighbor affinity and DT map are canonical tasks in connectomics field, but using a shared backbone to predict also a centerline/skeleton map is quite interesting. The system explicitly models “confidence” in a specific channel of EM visual representation, which seems to address a key issue in connectomics dataset(blurry and long tail corner cases are harder vs clear/sharp boundaries, and different types of corner case may require different cues) The second stage uses a residual pathway to isolate stage-1’s affinity map and effectively trains the BRR module to learn the finer grained details. This seems quite effective according to the reported ablations.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: ACWM seems to allow better convergence, but the lambda weights are manually determined, wondering if there was a more principled method, or would be better if trainable/gated in stage 1 as well Evaluation is constrained on smaller test data cubes that has been around for a while, would be nice to see some benchmarks on larger scale, especially long range neurite continuity type of benchmarks
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem in large-scale connectomics. The overall framework is fairly complete and integrates affinity learning, structure-aware auxiliary supervision, refinement, and model compression in a coherent way. The focus on stability and efficiency is relevant.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The methodological novelty appears limited, as several proposed components seem closer to standard engineering integrations than to clearly distinct methodological advances. Some parts of the pipeline are also not described clearly enough, and the absence of a validation set raises concern that some reported settings may depend on fortunate hyperparameter choices. More explicit reporting of hyperparameter settings would also improve reproducibility.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Area Chair and reviewers for their careful evaluation of our manuscript. We are grateful that the paper was selected for provisional acceptance. We provide below a concise point-by-point clarification of the main methodological, experimental, and presentation issues that may benefit from a more precise statement in the camera-ready version. R1-W1: We clarify that the pruning module aims to eliminate inter-feature redundancy to satisfy the rigorous deployment demands of terabyte-scale connectomics. To better justify its practical value beyond theoretical FLOPs, we will discuss the FLOPs-latency distinction and add practical inference latency comparisons to Table 4 in the camera-ready version. R1-W2: We thank the reviewer for this insightful observation. While 3D skeleton computation is indeed intensive, it is a one-time offline preprocessing step applied only to annotated training data and fully bypassed during inference on massive unlabeled EM volumes, thus preserving terabyte-scale scalability. Given the critical need for topological correctness, this one-time training overhead is a worthwhile trade-off. We will discuss it on massive neuron segmentation tasks in the camera-ready version. R1-W3: We sincerely thank the reviewer for appreciating the ingenuity of our ACWM and BRR designs. We respectfully clarify that our multi-task architecture introduces minimal training overhead. The predictions share a unified backbone with lightweight parallel output heads, and the BRR module adds only marginal parameters. We will update Table 4 and the Implementation Details with comprehensive metrics to empirically demonstrate this efficiency. R1-W4&5: Our framework is a single cascaded pipeline, not two independent models. “Ours (S-I)” evaluates the intermediate output directly from the Stage-I backbone, while “Ours (S-II)” evaluates the final output of the complete framework. The identical parameter counts in Table 4 are unfortunately a clerical error, which we will correct with accurate parameters and FLOPs in the camera-ready version. R2-W1: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion and apologize for the confusion caused by our terminology. When we used the term “fixed scalars” in the manuscript, we intended to describe the stabilizing and normalizing role of these parameters during the training process, rather than implying they were manually selected. Inspired by the work [1], our task weights are formulated as learnable uncertainty variables to automatically balance multiple loss terms. We will correct this terminology in the camera-ready version to eliminate any ambiguity. R2-W2: We fully agree. While current standard benchmarks enable fair comparisons, they do not capture the challenges of brain-scale, long-range neurite continuity. We will acknowledge this limitation and highlight large-scale continuity evaluation as an important future direction in the revision. R3-W1&2: To clarify, F_raw denotes the implicit features from the raw image, whereas A^ is the explicit Stage-I affinity prediction. Our design is not a standard engineering combination but a synergistic cross-modal fusion. The cascaded refinement uses the explicit structural prior to spatially guide and filter the implicit features, while the gradient-based pruning further exploits refined affinity gradients to eliminate false-positive connections, ensuring strict topological correctness. R3-W3&4: To prevent test-set leakage, our original implementation employed a separate validation set for model selection and tuning (the last 20 images of the 100-image AC4 dataset). Since the loss weights dynamically adapt to dataset variations to balance auxiliary losses, they lack a fixed range [1]. However, for exact reproducibility, both were initialized to 0.5.We will detail these settings in the camera-ready version. References: [1] Multi-task learning using uncertainty to weigh losses for scene geometry and semantics, In CVPR 2018.

title: Confidence-Aware Supervision for Robust Multi-task Embryo Grading
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper is well-motivated and delivers on what it sets out to do. The multitask learning framework is studied in considerable detail, jointly learning across three tasks whilst remaining sensitive to the varying levels of confidence throughout training. The paper is clearly structured and well written. The experimental evaluation is thorough and robust, examining performance across individual tasks as well as aggregated results, giving a comprehensive picture of the method’s behaviour. The discussion section is strong and demonstrates that the authors have a good understanding of their results and their implications.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The most significant limitation is the exclusive use of a private dataset, which severely limits reproducibility and generalisability. At a minimum, a publicly available dataset should have been included alongside the private one to allow for independent validation and fairer comparison with existing work. The paper is unnecessarily long due to the inclusion of standard formulations; the full equations for temperature scaling, predictive entropy, and ECE are well established and need only be cited. Relatedly, the prominence given to temperature scaling is disproportionate to its contribution. That temperature scaling improves calibration across all methods is entirely expected behaviour; it need only be noted as a standard post-hoc calibration step. Minor Points Standard ECE is used rather than KDE-ECE, which is the recommended calibration metric in the MICCAI community (Metrics reloaded: Recommendations for image analysis validation, 2022). ResNet-18 is a dated backbone; the authors should justify this choice. Several tables appear on incorrect pages.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The construction of a large dataset comprising 28,670 images collected from seven clinics for training and evaluation The approach effectively addresses the biological distinction between stage-specific requirements (global structure) and ICM/TE-specific requirements (local structure), translating the empirical knowledge accumulated by embryologists into a technical solution through multi-task learning uncertainty separation
reviewer_2_weaknesses: This study exclusively analyzes 2D static images captured at a single time point on the fifth day of culture, failing to leverage temporal developmental data or spatial embryonic information. While it employs ResNet18 as the backbone architecture, only the training methodology introduces novelty - the structural design itself shows no originality. No direct comparison is made with other multi-task learning (MTL) methods mentioned in the related works section. Although the separation between Stage and ICM/TE shows some improvement, there remains concern that the uncertainty separation between ICM and TE has not yet surpassed certain performance benchmarks. The paper’s explanations and presentation are reasonably clear, though it lacks an overarching figure that would provide better visual organization.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem The method is an improvement over naive label smoothing, as it improves both confidence calibration and prediction accuracy Extensive calibration metrics are reported to analyze the confidence improvement
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Increased training complexity by EMA and K-means purity clustering The method introduces several new hyperparameters that might have a sensitive effect on the training convergence The Methods section (§3) seems to be underspecified. I would not be able to faithfully reimplement the method with the provided information (see below)
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the clinical relevance, reliability-oriented evaluation, and methodological contribution of our work. A major concern raised by Reviewers #1 and #3 was reproducibility and missing implementation details. We agree that several aspects of the method can be clarified further. The 128-d feature projection is obtained using a learned linear layer from the 512-d ResNet backbone representation prior to clustering. Cluster purity is computed using ground-truth labels within each cluster, and K-means uses k-means++ initialization. Clustering is recomputed at each refinement stage using EMA features (decay=0.999). The entropy threshold was selected from τ ∈ {0.01, 0.02, 0.03}, and the number of refinement updates was searched within 3–7 based on validation performance. Due to space limitations, several implementation details were condensed in the current submission. Regarding dataset generalizability (R1/R2), although the dataset cannot be publicly released due to IRB and patient privacy constraints, it consists of 28,670 embryos collected from seven IVF clinics across multiple years with patient-independent splits. We emphasize that this is a multi-center heterogeneous dataset rather than a single-site cohort. The goal of this work was to study confidence reliability under heterogeneous grading uncertainty in realistic clinical settings. Our focus was reliability-aware supervision under standard Day-5 static image settings, where confidence behavior becomes clinically meaningful when heterogeneous grading outputs are jointly considered rather than evaluated independently. Reviewer #1 noted that temperature scaling (TS) was overemphasized. We agree that TS itself is a standard post-hoc calibration method and do not consider it a methodological contribution of this work. Rather, it was included to demonstrate that representation-level refinement and inference-time calibration act as complementary mechanisms. Accordingly, the primary objective of the proposed framework is not large classification accuracy gains, but reducing overconfident behavior while preserving discriminative performance under heterogeneous uncertainty. Regarding the lack of comparison with other MTL approaches (R2), existing MTL balancing methods primarily focus on gradient or loss balancing across tasks, whereas our objective is different: improving confidence reliability under heterogeneous uncertainty. Our framework selectively refines supervision based on confidence stability rather than optimizing task weights. Therefore, the proposed method is orthogonal to conventional MTL balancing approaches. For the choice of ResNet18 (R1/R2), we intentionally used a lightweight and well-established backbone to isolate the effect of the proposed confidence-aware supervision strategy from architectural improvements. Our goal was not to introduce a new architecture, but to demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves reliability behavior under a standard MTL setting. Regarding method complexity and hyperparameter sensitivity (R3), we observed relatively stable behavior across the explored τ range and update counts. Since refinement is performed only a few times during training, the additional computational overhead remains modest. Finally, we appreciate the suggestions regarding KDE-ECE, overall figure organization, formatting consistency, and clearer presentation of task-specific performance behaviors.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Paper summary: This paper proposes a multitask learning framework for embryo grading that incorporates a confidence-aware soft labeling scheme to improve model robustness under heterogeneous uncertainty. The method is evaluated on a private dataset of day-five embryos, and the authors further demonstrate that temperature scaling improves model calibration. Strengths: The reviewers identified several strengths, including: Well-motivated and clearly presented, with a principled confidence-aware multi-task learning framework. Clinically relevant and biologically grounded, effectively modeling global and local embryo characteristics. Large-scale multi-center dataset (28,670 images from seven clinics), enabling robust evaluation. Comprehensive experiments, including task-level, overall, and calibration analyses. Improved accuracy and confidence calibration, outperforming naive label smoothing approaches. Weaknesses: The main concerns raised by reviewers include: Limited reproducibility and generalizability, as evaluation is conducted exclusively on a private dataset without validation on a public benchmark. Methodological novelty is moderate, with improvements stemming mainly from the training strategy rather than the backbone/model architecture, and lacking direct comparison with prior multi-task learning methods. Limited modeling scope, relying only on single-timepoint 2D images without leveraging temporal developmental dynamics or richer spatial information. Increased complexity and reproducibility concerns due to additional hyperparameters, EMA/K-means components, and insufficient methodological detail for faithful reimplementation. Presentation can be improved, including conciseness, clearer visual organization, and stronger justification of design choices (e.g., backbone selection, evaluation metrics). Decision: The paper has clear strengths, but several substantive concerns remain unresolved, particularly regarding reproducibility and generalizability, comparison with prior multi-task learning methods, and the presentation of the paper. These points appear addressable through author clarification. I therefore recommend Invite for Rebuttal. | Thank you for the detailed and constructive rebuttal. The responses addressed the main concerns raised during review and improved confidence in both the methodological clarity and experimental setup. In particular, the authors clarified several previously missing implementation details related to feature projection, clustering, refinement strategy, hyperparameter selection, and training stability, substantially improving reproducibility. The rebuttal also clarified the motivation and scope of the work, improving confidence reliability under heterogeneous clinical uncertainty rather than maximizing classification performance or introducing a new architecture. The explanation of the multi-center dataset design and patient-independent evaluation further strengthened confidence in the clinical relevance of the study. While some limitations remain, particularly regarding public data availability and broader comparisons with alternative MTL approaches, the current evidence supports the paper’s central claims and positions the contribution clearly within reliability-aware medical AI. I recommend authors to incorporate the clarified implementation details and improve presentation and reproducibility in the camera-ready version. My final recommendation is Accept. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper presents a confidence-aware supervision framework for multi-task embryo grading that aims to improve both predictive performance and confidence calibration under heterogeneous grading uncertainty. Reviewers highlighted the clinical relevance of the problem, large multi-center dataset, reliability-oriented evaluation, and comprehensive experimental analysis. The primary concerns are related to reproducibility, implementation details, comparison with existing multi-task learning approaches, and dataset availability. The rebuttal provided substantial clarification regarding the methodological details, training procedure, clustering strategy, hyperparameter selection, and rationale behind several design choices. While limitations remain regarding public data availability and broader benchmarking, these issues are understandable given the clinical setting and do not outweigh the strengths of the work. Overall, the paper addresses an important problem, demonstrates consistent improvements in reliability and calibration, and provides a meaningful contribution to confidence-aware learning in medical AI. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper aims to address an important problem with a well-motivated method and strong experimental validation. Strengthening the benchmark experiments and incorporating public dataset evaluations would significantly enhance the paper’s contribution.

title: ConstTrack: Constellation-Guided Cell Tracking Under Lineage Constraints
reviewer_1_strengths: Interesting cell tracking method, with two key novel components: constellation learning and delayed assignment. Thorough validation on two public data sets. Superior performance compared to state-of-the-art.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Presentation of the methodology needs more strictness.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Interesting approach that incorporates the local configuration of cells and their neighborhoods for the tracking decisions. End-to-end training of the entire tracking pipeline from detection to the tracked cells. Thorough validations on commonly used benchmark datasets like the cell tracking challenge.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The Deformnable DETR is used as the object detector; however, it is not fully clear if this is based on pre-trained weights or if the weights are entirely trained in your end-to-end training approach. The authors mention that as part of the auxiliary track metadata, the miss counter is stored. However, it is unclear what this miss counter actually contains and how it is being updated or defined. The Cell ID decoder fuses embeddings of the last states of the track; however, here it is not clear if all of the states are fused to one embedding or if the embeddings are still kept separate for the individual time points. Please comment or explain more thoroughly. For the parent assignment, there is also the class “no parent.” However, as long as there are some potential neighbors, I would guess that it’s always more likely to link one of these rather than not linking anything. Is there any threshold or other cue included that would favor the “no parent” decision over the existing neighbors in the potential parent list? Please comment on that or explain how the “no parent” class is becoming more likely. The authors mentioned that the cell detections are rasterized in order to be able to use the TRA metric of the Cell Tracking Challenge. Does this imply that you are using rectangular segmentations for the tracking validation? In your ablations, you show that K > 6 decreases the quality. How about using smaller K values, which means less neighbors? Is 6 already the sweet spot? The authors show that removing the neighborhood constellation altogether yields poor results on one dataset; however, it is unclear how this would affect the outcome on different datasets. So it would be interesting to additionally extend the ablations to all of the other datasets for a more valid proof (e.g. as supplementary table). Generally, the ablation studies seem a bit cherry-picked and only focus on demonstrations on selected datasets. Unfortunately, there is no software or repository shared or mentioned, which potentially makes it difficult or impossible to perfectly reproduce the results. Please consider sharing your algorithm upon acceptance of the paper. Minor comments: The title of the paper you’re using title case; however, in all the sub-sections you’re using sentence case. Maybe make this more consistent by deciding for one or the other spelling. In Figure 1, you mentioned a grid on the input. Here, it is not clear to me where the grid is depicted in the figure. Maybe clarify or add it to the figure. How is the halo overlap between different regions defined, and which explicit size do you use for your experiments? Is the detection of duplicates potentially impacted by false positives and false negatives that you might observe with your detection approach?
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The authors proposed to boost the performance of cell tracking with contextual information from neighbouring detections. The appearance drift of cells in dense scenes can hopefully be solved because of the increased information window. The parent ID of each cell was therefore inferred from mixed features directly. Extensive experiments were conducted to show the superiority of their framework.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: While this work is relatively interesting regarding the methodology, a few comments are listed as follows for reference: 1.The Figure 1 does not match with the content of methodology. The features of appearance and geometry are not added directly. 2.For track-pool memory, track stack T_t^m is not referred to in the following sections. Is the framework stable with different deltas? How is the information of different “state” formulated? 3.How is the one-to-one association regularized? 4.For the quantitative results in Table 1, what is the meaning of BF-C2DL-MuSC, DIC-C2DH-HeLa… 5.For the ablation study, I don’t think the number of previous frame L is the key point. Experiments on the effectiveness of Track-pool memory, delta, composition of appearance/geometry features are considerably necessary.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their comments and assessment. In the camera-ready version, we will improve clarity, reproducibility, and presentation with concise revisions under the strict page limit. We will add a public repository with code and more qualitative results. R1-C1: Notation/parameters. We will clean notation to avoid confusing symbol and clarify variables essential to the algorithm. The main text will report key settings; complete hyperparameters and configurations will be provided in the repository. R1-C2: Figure readability. We agree with the reviewer. We will revise Fig. 1 to improve readability, enlarge the visual components where possible. R2-C1: Detector initialization. Deformable DETR is trained from scratch, no ImageNet- or COCO-pretrained weights are used for the ResNet-50 backbone or detector components. The detector, constellation encoder, ID decoder, and parent head are optimized jointly. R2-C2: Miss counter. The miss counter is the number of consecutive frames without assignment. It is reset to 0 when matched, initialized to 0 for newborn tracks, and incremented when unmatched. Tracks with miss <= delta are eligible for ID prediction; older tracks remain for lineage bookkeeping. R2-C3: Last L states. The track-pool memory keeps each track history, but historical states are not separate identity candidates. For association, the most recent L states of each eligible track are aggregated into one track token; the decoder scores one token per track plus newborn. R2-C4: No-parent. No-parent is an explicit class in the (P+1)-way parent classifier, supervised by newborn detections that are not division children. During delayed decision, the full (P+1)-class logits, including no-parent, are accumulated. If no-parent has the maximum score, no parent edge is added. R2-C5: CTC rasterisation. Yes, predicted boxes are rasterised as rectangular instance-labelled proxy masks only and to satisfy the official CTC input format. They are not pixel-accurate segmentations, so we report TRA and Cell-HOTA but not SEG. R2-C6: Ablations and K value. The paper reports the most diagnostic examples. Fluo-N2DH-GOWT1 is used for constellation and K because it stresses dense local association; PhC-C2DH-U373 is used for history length because it tests temporal association. K=6 is motivated by six-neighbour topology in dense 2D cell layers and selected by our K validation. R2-C7: Halo tiling. For dense or large-FOV sequences, halo tiling is used in training and inference to fit detector computation in GPU memory while preserving boundary context. Tile width/overlap are fixed per dataset/cell type. At inference, tile detections are mapped globally and duplicates in overlaps are merged before tracking. FP/FN remain detector errors. R2-C8: Repository/minor issues. We will add the repository link, use consistent heading capitalization, and Fig. 1 will be revised to be more visually explicit. R3-C1: Fig. 1 fusion. Eq. (2) fuses appearance and geometry after learned linear projections; Fig. 1 used a simplified illustration. We will show this step more explicitly. R3-C2: Track memory/delta. Each track stores its history of detection states, only the most recent L states of eligible tracks are retrieved for ID prediction. Delta defines eligibility; older tracks are retained for lineage bookkeeping. R3-C3: Dataset names. The dataset names follow the CTC naming convention: the prefix indicates imaging modality and dimensionality, such as BF, DIC, Fluo, or PhC, and the suffix denotes the cell type or sequence, such as HSC, MuSC, HeLa, GOWT1, U373, or PSC. R3-C4: Ablation scope. We will revise the ablation wording to make clear that the paper reports representative ablations rather than exhaustive dataset-wise tables. The reported examples are selected to test the corresponding ambiguity: dense local association for the constellation module and temporal association for short track-history memory.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a cell tracking approach leveraging the spatial context information and temporal lineage constraint. Reviewers confirmed the experiment performances. But, a long list of comments was also provided by three reviewers. Authors need to address them in the final submission. The three reviewers gave >=4 review scores and the AC agreed with the recommendation.

title: Cross-Cancer Expert-Routing Knowledge Transfer in Federated Prognosis Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: The problem is important and clinically relevant. Prognosis prediction for rare or data-scarce cancers is exactly where transfer learning can help, but negative transfer across cancer types is a real concern. The combination of parameter-efficient expert learning and target-adaptive routing is well matched to the problem setting and more targeted than learning a single monolithic pan-cancer model. The empirical study is broad: five target cancers, three MIL backbones, few-shot evaluation, and component ablations.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Some of the result claims are too strong. FedERF is the best method on average, but not uniformly across every target and backbone. For example, on ABMIL-LIHC it is slightly below Scratch, and on WiKG-UCEC it does not exceed ROUPKT. Claims such as ‘consistently outperforms’ should therefore be softened. 2.The algorithmic schedule needs to be written more clearly. Eq. (1) reads like a joint optimization of the global backbone and expert parameters, while the text describes first training w_G and then freezing w_G to learn the LoRA experts. The two-stage procedure should be made explicit.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem: prognosis prediction for rare or data-scarce cancers from WSIs, where both limited target data and cross-cancer heterogeneity create major challenges for robust modeling. 2.The proposed method is well motivated conceptually. The decomposition into federated expert construction and target-adaptive routing aligns naturally with the stated goal of leveraging transferable pan-cancer priors while reducing negative transfer from irrelevant cancers. 3.FedERF shows strong overall empirical performance, achieving the best reported average C-index across all three backbones, which suggests that the framework is broadly effective rather than tied to a single architecture. 4.The ablation study is informative and supports the proposed design. Removing experts, averaging experts without routing, or replacing pretrained experts with random ones all degrades performance relative to the full model, indicating that both the expert pool and the adaptive routing mechanism contribute meaningfully.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The evaluation setting and the use of the term “federated” would benefit from clearer explanation. The experiments appear to model federation across cancer cohorts in a leave-one-out cross-cancer transfer setting, but the manuscript does not clearly discuss what kind of federation is being modeled and how this setting should be interpreted relative to more conventional FL scenarios. 2.The novelty relative to prior cross-cancer transfer and routing-based methods could be positioned more sharply. While the paper argues that monolithic global models cause negative transfer and introduces expert routing as the solution, the precise methodological distinction from prior transfer/routing paradigms is not articulated as clearly as it could be. 3.Some baseline definitions are under-explained. In particular, Scratch serves as an important reference in Table 1, but the manuscript does not clearly define whether it means target-only training from random initialization, from pretrained backbone weights, or under exactly matched training budgets, making the comparison harder to interpret precisely. 4.The choice of ROUPKT as a key baseline is not sufficiently motivated in the paper’ s earlier positioning. Although it is included in experiments and adapted to the current setting, it is not introduced in the motivation/background discussion in Sec. 1, so the reader lacks context for why this is a particularly relevant comparison and how it conceptually relates to FedERF. 5.The empirical validation would be stronger with more statistical support and implementation detail. The paper reports means and standard deviations and includes useful ablations, but it does not provide stronger significance analysis or enough architecture-specific details about expert/router insertion and training configuration to fully assess robustness and reproducibility.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Unlike conventional slide-level routers, the proposed Layer-wise Dynamic Routing Mechanism operates at the patch level across different layers. This allows for a more “target-tailored” expert routing, which is particularly effective for capturing the heterogeneous nature of cancer across different clients in a federated setting. While the individual components may not represent entirely new concepts, the study presents a sophisticated integration of existing principles to significantly advance the performance ceiling of federated MIL. It can be interpreted as a well-executed, progressive approach to local model customization. The authors effectively demonstrate the versatility of FedERF by testing it across various backbone architectures. This empirical validation proves the framework’s utility as a plug-and-play solution that is not restricted to a specific feature extractor.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The overview of the training workflow in Figure 1 is difficult to follow. The mixture of “Phase 1/2” labels with separate numbered markers (1, 2, 3) and multi-directional connections creates visual confusion. A more linear or modular layout would be necessary for readers to grasp the system architecture clearly. The mathematical formulations, such as Equation (5), suffer from an excessive number of superscripts and subscripts, hindering immediate comprehension. Rather than dedicating space to standard LoRA formulations (Equation 3), the authors should focus on simplifying and clarifying the notations for their core proposed mechanisms. There is a discrepancy in terminology between the “Preliminary” section (Phase 1 & 2) and the rest of the manuscript. This inconsistency, combined with a lack of detailed implementation parameters, makes the study difficult to reproduce without the original source code. The process by which a target client initializes from global weights and retrieves from the expert pool is inadequately explained. Without a clear description of the retrieval logic, the claim that the model becomes “cancer-specific” lacks sufficient justification. Beyond numerical performance gains, the paper provides little evidence of cancer-specific learning. The authors should include qualitative evaluations or case studies where patch-level and layer-level routing show distinct, interpretable differences to support their claims. The experimental results indicate high sensitivity to hyperparameter changes. This suggests that the model may require extensive site-specific optimization, which could limit its practical scalability in diverse federated environments.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal

title: D2C: Data-Efficient Skin Lesion Classification for Clinical Images by Representation Alignment Using Dermoscopic Resources
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The approach addresses an important and practical problem. 2.The method demonstrates encouraging classification performance, as evidenced by improvements in AUROC over the baselines. 3.The manuscript is well-written and organized.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The proposed framework involves a two-stage training procedure. However, the computational complexity, in terms of both training and inference time, is not discussed. A comparison with baseline methods in terms of efficiency would strengthen the practical relevance of the method. 2.The process for selecting hyperparameters (e. g. , parameters a and b, and the balancing coefficients) is not described. 3.The evaluation of classification performance is limited to AUROC. Including additional metrics would provide a more comprehensive assessment of the model’s performance. 4.It is unclear whether the baseline results were reproduced or directly taken from the original papers. This should be explicitly stated to ensure fairness and comparability of the evaluation.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper addresses an important real-world problem, bridging the gap between dermoscopic images and clinical photos used in practice. 2.The use of class-aware feature vaults is a good idea, helping stable feature learning and improving alignment and contrastive learning beyond normal batch methods. 3.The combination of multiple alignment techniques (centroid, contrastive, FFT mixing, consistency) is well designed and effective for handling domain shifts like lighting and color changes. 4.The method is practical for clinical use as it works well with very few labeled target samples (5–10%). 5.The evaluation is strong, with multiple datasets, low-label settings, good baselines, and clear ablation studies.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The novelty is limited, as most components are already known and the main contribution is their combination. 2.The evaluation is limited to binary classification, with no results for multi-class or imbalanced real-world scenarios. 3.The target datasets are merged without proper analysis, and separate results are not reported. 4.Important baselines (source-only, target-only, mixed training) and statistical tests are missing, making it harder to fully judge the gains.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: (1) The experimental results show that this method is effective. (2) The ways of applying Fast Fourier Transform and contrastive learning between the source and target domains are somewhat interesting.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: In the introduction, the authors emphasize data quantity imbalance as an essential challenge. However, it is not sufficiently clear how the proposed method specifically addresses this issue. In addition, the potential influence of batch-based computation or batch composition is not discussed. Moreover, the unlabeled images appear to be used in a fully unsupervised or self-supervised manner. To some extent, this makes the proposed framework resemble existing self-supervised representation learning methods, such as BYOL, which have also shown strong performance under semi-supervised fine-tuning protocols. Therefore, a more explicit discussion of the relation between the proposed method and existing self-supervised / semi-supervised approaches would help clarify the novelty and significance of the work.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We greatly appreciate all reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive feedback. As follows, we will address the raised concerns. R1C1 Computational complexity. Inference time is crucial for clinical use. DivAug requires two forward passes, whereas the rest, including our method, require only one. Thus, our method achieves either faster or equivalent inference time compared to others, given identical classifiers. The first-stage training of a ResNet-18 on the selected ISIC-2017 under the paper settings takes 40 minutes. This stage only needs to be trained once and requires no future retraining. Hence, we believe the cost is sufficiently acceptable. We did not observe significant differences in training time in the second stage compared to others, as the methods differ primarily in their loss function designs. We will add a discussion about this. R1C2 Hyperparameters. They are selected based on experiments and typical values. For instance, the balancing factors are picked from 0.001 to 1, scaled by 10 each time. a is selected from 0.1 to 0.4 and b from 0.6 to 0.9.We will add a proper description of this. R1C3 Evaluation metric. We choose AUROC because it is the most comprehensive metric for skin lesion classification, accounting for data imbalance and different thresholds. Still, we acknowledge the usefulness of additional metrics. We will keep this in mind and apply it for future work. R1C4 Baseline results. All baseline results are reproduced. ReCo, FCAT, and SAT-DA involve skin image datasets but have misaligned dataset and task settings. Hence, we have to reproduce them in our uniform setting. All the other methods were using natural image datasets, making reproduction necessary. We will also add a description of this. R2C1, R2C2, R3C2 Method positioning, novelty. Our method is a semi-supervised domain adaptation approach that emphasizes domain adaptation, as leveraging dermoscopic resources for clinical images is clinically meaningful. The two lesion types in the datasets, nevus and melanoma, are imbalanced in quantity. Hence, the clinical task we address is differentiating melanoma from nevus using imbalanced data, a challenging and practical clinical problem. Since the data imbalance already exists in the datasets, we believe the evaluation results can reflect performance in real-world scenarios. The semi-supervised aspect arises because there are always unlabeled clinical images, which can be leveraged to improve performance. Based on our experiments, L_cdfc and L_fcui have effectively leveraged them, whereas overly complex semi-supervised schemes have adversely affected the performance. Methods such as BYOL are primarily for pure self-supervised representation learning to obtain general backbones, which we believe is not very relevant to our paper. We will add a further discussion for clarification. R2C3 Dataset merging. Too few test data lead to a more biased evaluation. Therefore, we merge the datasets to increase the test data size, enhancing the convincingness of the experimental results. We will add a description of this. R2C4 Baseline issue. The first setting in Sec. 3.3 uses labeled source images and 5% labeled target images, and our full method delivers a significant gain compared to it. The source-only and target-only settings will be inferior to the first setting, as they only use partial data. We believe this issue does not affect the convincingness of our method. R3C1 Data use. The large number of dermoscopic images in the Introduction is mentioned to introduce vault-based computation for L_cara and L_iwca. L_cara aims to align the feature centroids, where the centroid estimates are more accurate with more feature samples. L_iwca uses contrastive learning, which performs better with larger sample sizes. We agree that the description of this part needs refinement. Also, it would be beneficial to perform additional ablation studies for this. We will apply them in future work.
