title: DLCE-MIL: Depth-aware Local Context Enhanced Multiple Instance Learning for Patient-Level IVCM Fungal Keratitis Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically important and genuinely underexplored problem. Fusarium versus Aspergillus subtype classification from IVCM is a fine-grained task with direct treatment implications, and no prior work has applied a patient-level MIL framework to this specific problem. The dataset of 127 patients with culture-confirmed genus-level labels is the largest reported for this subtyping task, and the experimental design is sound with proper patient-level 5-fold stratified cross-validation preventing data leakage. The two proposed components are well motivated by the clinical acquisition structure of IVCM. The depth-aware fusion directly addresses a gap explicitly identified in prior fungal keratitis classification work as a missing capability. The ablation study in Table 2 systematically evaluates each component individually and in combination, providing clear evidence of the contribution of each module to the final performance. The comparison against both general MIL frameworks and keratitis-specific baselines is comprehensive within the scope of the paper.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper’s core motivation is that IVCM acquisition sequences are ordered and prior MIL methods wrongly treat them as unordered sets. Towards Interpretable, Sequential Multiple Instance Learning: An Application to Clinical Imaging (Luo, Wang, and Li, PMC12919601) introduces BiSMIL, a bidirectional Transformer that directly addresses this problem by systematically incorporating the sequential nature of clinical imaging into MIL. The authors compare against ABMIL, CLAM, and TransMIL but do not include BiSMIL. Since the paper’s entire motivation rests on the sequential structure argument, this is a significant omission. 2.Reducing Variability of Multiple Instance Learning Methods for Digital Pathology (Mammadov, Le Folgoc, Hocquet, and Gori, Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention MICCAI 2025, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 15966, Springer) documents that MIL methods suffer from performance variability across runs reaching up to 10 to 15 AUC points, stemming from weight initialization, batch ordering, and learning rate. The claimed improvement of DLCE-MIL over TransMIL is only 3.4 AUC points, which falls within this documented variability range. No fixed random seeds, multi-seed averaging, or statistical significance testing is reported, making it impossible to confirm the claimed improvement is significant in real. 3.AI-Based Decision-Support System for Diagnosing Acanthamoeba Keratitis Using In Vivo Confocal Microscopy Images (Lincke, Roth, Macedo, Bergman, Lowe, and Lagali, Translational Vision Science and Technology, 2023) addresses structural challenges of IVCM sequences in the same imaging modality using Heidelberg HRT-RCM, explicitly sorting images into corneal layers before patient-level diagnosis. This paper is neither cited, nor discussed. The authors should revise their related work to accurately scope their novelty claims. 4.DINOv2-Small is used as a frozen feature extractor in all experiments, with no ablation comparing frozen versus fine-tuned configurations, no size variants tested, and no justification provided for this design choice. 5.The dataset contains 75 Fusarium versus 52 Aspergillus patients. With 5-fold cross-validation, each test fold contains approximately 10 Aspergillus patients. Per-class performance breakdown is not reported, no class-imbalance correction is applied, and no statistical significance testing is provided. The overlapping confidence intervals in Table 1 and Table 2 make it difficult to determine whether DLCE-MIL reliably outperforms TransMIL, particularly for the minority Aspergillus class. 6.The gated scalar alpha initialized to 0 is an interesting design choice, but the converged value of alpha after training is not reported. The ablation shows only aggregate metrics with no per-class breakdown showing whether depth fusion specifically helps Fusarium or Aspergillus classification. No perturbation test on depth values at test time is performed, so it cannot be confirmed the model genuinely exploits depth information.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Novel Formulation for IVCM: The authors effectively translate the clinical reality of non-monotonic IVCM acquisition into a structured MIL problem, moving beyond the standard “bag-of-images” assumption to model axial continuity. 2.Integration of Physical Priors: Using learnable depth embeddings to modulate latent representations is a technically sound way to leverage metadata that is often ignored in purely visual models. 3.Strong Clinical Feasibility: The use of a frozen DINOv2 backbone demonstrates a data-efficient approach suitable for medical domains where labeled samples are scarce, while still achieving state-of-the-art performance (79.32% accuracy) on a large-scale clinical dataset.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Lack of External Validation: The dataset is restricted to only two fungal genera (Fusarium and Aspergillus) from a single-center cohort. Performance is reported solely via 5-fold cross-validation on the internal dataset. Without testing on data from different institutions or different IVCM device models, the model’s robustness to domain shift remains unverified. 2.Superficial Qualitative Evidence: The paper lacks visual interpretability results (such as attention maps or saliency analysis) to confirm that the model is focusing on hyphal morphologies rather than imaging artifacts or background noise. 3.Incremental Nature of LICE: The LICE module is essentially a 1D convolutional layer added to a standard TransMIL architecture. While effective, the technical novelty of applying 1D-Conv for local context is relatively limited in the broader context of sequence modeling. 4.Sensitivity to Depth Noise: The depth fusion mechanism relies on the accuracy of clinician-entered depth values. The paper does not provide a robustness analysis or a “noisy depth” simulation to determine how much performance degrades if the physical depth metadata is imprecise.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Strengths: (1) Strong clinical motivation and problem formulation. Differentiating Fusarium and Aspergillus is a real, practical clinical need for determining targeted antifungal therapy. Framing the analysis of IVCM sequences as a patient-level MIL problem is a natural and effective fit for this specific imaging modality. (2) Architecture tailored to IVCM physics. I appreciate that the authors did not simply plug in an off-the-shelf MIL model, but rather designed the network around the actual acquisition characteristics of IVCM. The LICE module breaks the standard IID assumption in traditional MIL. Using 1D convolutions to capture local tissue continuity between adjacent slices is a computationally lightweight but effective way to model short-range structures like hyphae networks. The depth-aware fusion is a clever approach to handling the non-monotonic nature of clinical scanning. Mapping physical depth to a learnable embedding to conditionally modulate the visual features makes intuitive sense. Additionally, initializing the learnable scalar α\alphaα to 0 is a nice, practical touch that allows the model to stabilize on visual features before incorporating depth constraints. (3) Solid and rigorous evaluation. The experimental setup is methodologically sound. While the dataset size is moderate, the authors correctly implement a strict patient-level 5-fold cross-validation. This is crucial for this type of sequential data to prevent slice-level data leakage, making the reported metrics reliable. Furthermore, the ablation study in table 2 is straightforward and clearly isolates the contributions of the LICE and depth fusion modules.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Weaknesses: (1) In Section 2.3, the authors claim that initializing α=0\alpha=0α=0 improves stability under “missing depth values.” However, they explicitly state in Section 3.2 that there are zero missing depth values in their dataset. Since this was never empirically tested, the claim is entirely speculative. The authors should either remove this claim or demonstrate it by artificially masking depth values during training. (2) There is a disconnect between Figure 1 and the mathematical formulations in the text. Figure 1 explicitly illustrates a “Squaring” operation before the depth-aware fusion. While I recognize this is likely the spatial sequence reshaping step required by the TransMIL backbone (specifically to feed 1D sequences into the 2D PPEG module), the authors completely fail to mention or mathematically define this step in Sections 2.2 or 2.3.Readers unfamiliar with TransMIL’s internal mechanics will find this confusing. (3) The manuscript contains glaring errors that detract from the professional quality of the work. For instance, in Figure 1, “Module” is misspelled as “Moudel” in the LICE header. The authors must thoroughly proofread the text and figures. (4) While the strict patient-level 5-fold CV is appreciated, the standard deviations reported in Tables 1 and 2 are quite high (e.g., an F1-Score of 0.7494 ±\pm± 0.0968 for the proposed method). This instability is likely a consequence of the relatively small patient cohort (N=127). The authors need to explicitly acknowledge this high variance and discuss the limitations of their dataset size in the Discussion/Conclusion section. (5) The paper uses a private clinical dataset of 127 patients but completely lacks any statement regarding IRB approval, ethics committee review, or patient informed consent. This is a critical omission for a clinical application paper submitted to MICCAI. (6) No code or dataset link is provided. Given the custom LICE and depth-fusion implementations, providing access to the code is highly recommended to verify the methodology.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the clinical significance of our work and IVCM-tailored architecture. CQ1 Statistical significance and variability (R1, R3) : To address MIL run-to-run variability, we re-evaluated TransMIL and DLCE-MIL across 3 random seeds. Multi-seed AUC was 0.7682±0.0167 for TransMIL and 0.8135±0.0185 for DLCE-MIL, with significant improvement confirmed by a paired t-test (p=0.0187). CQ2 Depth/alpha (R1, R2, R3) : The learned α moved away from zero and converged to ~0.1, suggesting that depth information was utilized. A noisy-depth perturbation only slightly decreased ACC from 0.7932 to 0.7845, indicating that depth acts as a lightweight auxiliary modulation without causing over-reliance on metadata. CQ3 “Squaring” (R1, R3): “Squaring” follows the original TransMIL terminology and refers to padding N tokens to S^2 tokens with S=ceil(sqrt(N)), followed by reshaping into a pseudo-spatial S x S grid before PPEG, not element-wise squaring. We will define this in Sec. 2.4 and correct “Moudel” to “Module”. CQ4 Ethics/code (R1, R2, R3): We apologize for omitting the ethics statement. This retrospective study used anonymized IVCM data and complies with institutional ethical guidelines for clinical data analysis. Privacy restrictions prevent sharing raw images; however, we will open-source the core codebase upon publication, including LICE, depth fusion, and the training pipeline. R1 F1-score: After rechecking the logs, we found a transcription error in the ablation table: the F1-score of the depth-fusion-only variant was incorrectly entered, creating the misleading impression that the full model had a lower F1-score. We apologize for this oversight and have corrected the table in the revision. The corrected table removes this apparent inconsistency. R1 related work/baselines : We will discuss the suggested studies, including BiSMIL, MIL run-to-run variability, and IVCM-based clinical decision-support works using corneal layer or sequence information. BiSMIL targets bidirectional sequential MIL and early prediction, whereas DLCE-MIL focuses on depth-aware patient-level IVCM fungal subtype classification. We did not include BiSMIL quantitatively because it targets bidirectional sequential MIL and early prediction, which differs from our patient-level IVCM subtype classification setting, and no suitable official implementation was available for faithful adaptation. R1 DINOv2 : For the backbone concern, we additionally tested frozen DINOv2-Base and fine-tuned DINOv2-Small, which achieved ACC=0.74 and ACC=0.76, respectively; both were below frozen DINOv2-Small, supporting our choice for the limited grayscale IVCM dataset. R2 external validation: The dataset was acquired using Heidelberg Retina Tomograph III, a mainstream IVCM device. We acknowledge the single-center/single-device limitation and will add it to the Limitations section; multicenter, multi-device validation is future work. R2 interpretability: We added representative DINOv2 CLS-attention heatmaps for Fusarium and Aspergillus cases, showing that the model mainly attends to corneal structural regions rather than background. R2 LICE novelty: LICE is not a generic 1D convolution operator , but as task-aware local context modeling tailored to IVCM acquisition. It explicitly captures neighboring-slice continuity before global MIL aggregation, complementing TransMIL and improving fungal subtype recognition. R3 variance/limitations : We agree that the relatively high standard deviations are related to the small cohort size (N=127). We explicitly acknowledge this variance and dataset-size limitation in the added Limitations section.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers recognize the clinical significance of differentiating fungal keratitis subtypes (Fusarium vs. Aspergillus) and appreciate the thoughtfully designed framework tailored to the specific physics of IVCM imaging. title: DualCaMIL: Dual-Level Causal Multi-instance Learning for Patient-Level Diagnosis in Reflectance Confocal Microscopy
reviewer_1_strengths: The motivation to mitigate confounding factors is important for improving robustness and generalization in medical AI. Leveraging histopathology images as a cross-modal reference to guide RCM representation learning is an interesting idea.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The study is limited to basal cell carcinoma diagnosis using RCM. Although the proposed method appears broadly applicable, its generalizability to other tasks and datasets is not evaluated. Relatedly, the effectiveness of the patient-level causal modeling module is only validated on a single task, and should be further assessed across diverse settings. Most competing methods are relatively simple MIL baselines. Stronger comparisons with domain-invariant or causality-based learning approaches are needed. A clearer conceptual comparison with existing domain-invariant learning methods would help justify the advantages of the proposed approach. The paper uses several unclear or unconventional terms (e. g. , “patient instances”), which makes some technical details difficult to follow.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful and technically challenging setting of patient-level diagnosis from multiple RCM images with only patient-level labels. The proposed dual-level formulation is well motivated. The instance-level CMCD module and patient-level PMCM module target different confounding mechanisms rather than using a single generic invariance objective. The quantitative results are strong relative to the listed baselines. In Table 1, the method improves over TransMIL, MicroMIL, and IRM, and the ablation in Table 2 supports that both proposed components contribute. The paper includes patient-level counterfactual stress tests in addition to standard classification metrics which is a useful robustness analysis and strengthens the empirical story beyond reporting a single AUC. The clinical motivation and overall pipeline are clearly communicated and the paper makes a reasonable effort to connect the method design to domain-specific structural correspondence between RCM and histopathology.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: My main concern is that several methodological details necessary for confident interpretation and reproducibility are missing or insufficiently precise. The paper states that “label-matched pathology tiles provide teacher supervision for alignment,” but does not make clear whether the RCM pathology supervision is patient-matched, region-matched, or only class-matched. Given how central the cross-modal alignment is to the method, this ambiguity matters. Likewise the paper mentions orthogonality and reconstruction constraints in CMCD but the main text only writes out L_align and L_inv, leaving some key losses and their weights unspecified. A second important issue is that the causal framing is somewhat stronger than the evidence currently shown. The interventions in CMCD and the patient-subspace suppression in PMCM are plausible and useful design choices but the manuscript does not provide a formal causal model or an identifiability argument. This does not invalidate the method but it does suggest the claims should be framed more carefully as causally inspired robustness modeling rather than established causal identification. The private OOD evaluation is limited. The paper explicitly describes the private dataset as 86 BCC positive patients and uses it for OOD stress testing without fine-tuning. That makes the OOD robustness analysis directionally useful, but it does not support a standard out-of-distribution classification claim because no negative class performance is reported there. There appears to be a mismatch between the PMCM figure and the formal description. The text defines B_p through eigendecomposition of the patient covariance, while the figure visually suggests a context-encoder pathway. This should be reconciled. The manuscript does not report variability across runs, confidence intervals, or statistical testing, which makes it harder to judge the robustness of the reported improvements.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: DualCaMIL addresses spurious correlations in RCM diagnosis via a dual-level causal MIL framework that utilizes cross-modal microscopic disentanglement with histopathology references to eliminate imaging artifacts and a patient-aware macro-causal module to suppress individual background biases. The method demonstrates superior robustness and clinical relevance.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Minor: The text in the figures is too small and cannot be read clearly when printed. Major: Figure 1(a) can be understood, but the clustering trend in Figure 1(b) is not obvious. Please provide a clearer description. The paper mentions using label-matched histopathology patches for alignment. If the selected patches are of poor quality, or not from the same patient (although from the same disease type), how much impact would this have on the model’s disentanglement performance? Table 1 needs to evaluate results on three datasets; performance on a single dataset is insufficient to demonstrate effectiveness. Additionally, some other latest non-MIL testing methods need to be added, especially methods that have been validated on publicly available datasets.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank reviewers for recognizing DualCaMIL’s importance and promising results, and address the main concerns below. (i) Generalizability/datasets. DualCaMIL uses no BCC-specific handcrafted cues. It targets a broader patient-level MIL pattern: multiple images per patient, patient-level labels, style variation, and patient-shared background. This suggests broader applicability, but evidence validates patient-level RCM BCC diagnosis; we will narrow claims. One main classification dataset reflects task validity/public-data availability: valid testing needs RCM bags with patient-level positive/negative labels. Public RCM datasets matching this protocol are limited, and Monnier provides the target protocol. SkinCancer histopathology is not a second RCM test set; it provides cross-modal supervision motivated by RCM-H&E correspondence. The private RCM cohort is BCC-positive only; as R2 noted, it is not standard OOD classification, but no-finetuning stress testing under RCM domain shift. We acknowledge this limitation; broader patient-level MIL tasks and stronger compatible baselines are future work. (ii) Baselines/comparison. IRM seeks environment-level invariance, whereas patient-level RCM MIL involves two-level confounders: RCM style/artifacts affect individual instances, while site, pigmentation, scanning conditions, and tissue context can be shared within a patient bag. DualCaMIL addresses these separately through CMCD and PMCM, which differs from generic invariant learning. Many domain-invariant/causal methods require explicit environments, multi-environment training, or image/lesion labels unavailable in our setting. Preliminary experiments with several such methods also did not provide stable gains under this protocol. Thus Table 1 reports IRM as a compatible invariant-learning baseline and focuses on protocol-consistent MIL methods. (iii) Method clarity. “Patient instances” means multiple RCM images/patches forming one patient bag. Patient-level structural bias means stable same-patient background, e.g., site, texture, pigmentation, or tissue context, which naive MIL may mistake for evidence. For R2/R3’s pathology question, pathology supervision is class/semantic matched, not patient- or region-registered. CMCD uses pathology as a structural teacher, not paired registration; non-same-patient tiles need no spatial correspondence. Low-quality or semantically inconsistent tiles may weaken the teacher signal; semantic matching plus reconstruction, orthogonality, and intervention consistency mitigate, but do not eliminate, this risk. For R2’s PMCM figure concern, PMCM is defined in equations/text by eigendecomposition of the patient covariance matrix. Fig.2(c) only schematizes patient-context estimation/suppression, not an extra context encoder. We will clarify terminology, pathology matching, PMCM caption, and loss weights without changing the method. (iv) Claim calibration/causal interpretation. Evidence should not be read as formal causal identification. We retain the causality-driven framing because the method is motivated by intervention and counterfactual robustness, but will revise wording implying causal proof or identifiability. The supported claim is that DualCaMIL achieves mechanism-consistent robustness in ablation and PCST while preserving lesion sensitivity; it is not a formal causal theorem. (v) Reproducibility/statistics/presentation. We agree with R1/R2 that procedural details should be clearer. We will specify pathology selection/semantic matching, patient bag construction, PMCM k, CMCD losses/weights, training/inference flow, and PCST. Code will be released upon acceptance. Results are consistent across metrics/ablations/PCST; we will further explore repeated-run variability and statistical testing. For R3, Fig.1(b) is qualitative: each point is one patient-level embedding; dispersion shows naive pooling can amplify patient-specific background over lesion evidence. We will enlarge text and revise the caption.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: N/A Justification(s): There is broad agreement among the reviewers that the work addresses an important and relevant problem, and that the proposed solution is well-motivated and potentially useful with promising results. However, reviewers have highlighted issues with the methodology clarity, limitation to evaluating on a single dataset and unjustified interpretations. In rebuttal, the authors should (i) comment on the works generalizability to other tasks, include experimental results if they exist already; (ii) extend the comparison to more relevant baselines or justify limiting to the existing comparisons presented; (iii) similarly, include comparisons with other datasets if available or justify limiting to the single dataset used; (iv) clarify the methodology, including terms used; and (v) review the claims made to ensure that they are supported by the included results or provide additional justification. | N/A Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After rebuttal, this paper receives two accept recommendations and one rejection. The AC acknowledges that DualCaMIL addresses an important patient-level RCM diagnosis problem and proposes a well-motivated dual-level framework for mitigating instance- and patient-level confounding. Reviewers recognized the clinical relevance, promising empirical performance, and useful ablation and counterfactual stress-test analyses. The rebuttal clarifies several issues, including the scope of generalizability, the use of class/semantic-matched pathology supervision, the PMCM formulation, baseline selection, and the need to calibrate causal claims. However, substantial concerns remain regarding validation on only a single standard classification dataset, limited comparison with stronger causality/domain-invariant baselines, incomplete reproducibility details, and insufficient evidence for broader generalizability. Given that these limitations affect the strength of the main claims and cannot be fully resolved by presentation changes, the AC recommends rejection. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes DualCaMIL, a dual-level causality-driven MIL framework for RCM-based BCC diagnosis, addressing both instance-level and patient-level confounders. Reviewers find the method well-motivated, clinically relevant, and empirically strong against baselines, with meaningful ablations and counterfactual stress tests. While Reviewer #1 raises concerns about generalizability and baseline comparisons, Reviewers #2 and #3 see the contributions as solid and the rebuttal sufficiently addresses key issues. Recommendation: Accept.

title: Fast 3D Cell Volume Reconstruction from Multi-focus Images by Cross-modality Knowledge Distillation
reviewer_1_strengths: Compared to Deep Image Prior, the model provides a significant reduction in reconstruction time - enabling applications outside the scope of the prior art. The selection of models is appropriate for the task, and the methods are used within their scope.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The simulated multifocus images are consistent, but reconstructed volumes seem visually blurred. As the VAE forms a crucial part of the network, additional latent-space statistics could help confirm whether the model uses the latent variables effectively, as posterior collapse cannot be evaluated solely from the images. The stack is padded in z-direction from 11 to 12.A short clarification of how the padded slices are treated downstream would be helpful, as the percentage of added volume is not entirely negligible. While not in the main focus of the paper, short expansion on the cytological categories would be helpful, as they are referred to only as abbreviations. There is unnecessary repetition of dimensions in the beginning of Methodology, which likely could be compacted.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The work addresses a relevant problem. The idea to approximate the expensive reconstruction process and replacing it by an efficient deep learning based approach is sound, and the achieved runtime reduction is significant. The presentation is largely clear, with some minor issues (see below). However, I have several concerns regarding the used methodology and the evaluation, described below.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: My greatest concern is regarding the used methodology. While the use of a student teacher model generally appears feasible, it is entirely unclear to me why this relatively complex system of interacting models is necessary and superior over, for example, a simple U-Net model that predicts 3D volumes from multi-focus images end-to-end. I would expect to see the obtained results compared to such simpler models, which could then (potentially) motivate the use of the proposed pipeline. As currently presented, the complex pipeline is not justified. Along those lines: The authors recognize the lack of sharpness in the generated results, and attribute it to the probabilistic nature of the VAE (which I would agree on). However, as mentioned above, it is not clear to me why a probabilistic model is used in the first place, if the downstream application (i.e., reconstruction) is fully deterministic and does not require sampling. The differences in quality between the generated and DIP results are mentioned (e.g., intensity variations, blurieness), but the effect of these results are not appropriately discussed. Are these deviations from the groundtruth relevant in practice? Are the results usable like this? I would also like to raise concerns regarding the use of skip connections in the presented CellVAE architecture. As I understand, the purpose of the VAE is to capture the latent properties of the input. However, the skip connections effectively sabotage this objective, as information can freely flow more or less directly from input to output. Optimization wise, I would deem it counter productive to use skip connections in the VAE. I could not find a definition of a training and test set, and it was not specified on which data the metrics were computed. This should be clarified. Metrics computed on the training have little meaning to assess overall performance. I would expect more information on the used dataset. Is it an in-house dataset, or was a public dataset used? It would also benefit the paper to briefly explain what NILM, LSIL, HSIL, and SCC are to better understand the difference. Fig. 5 and 6 use different color maps. What is the reason for this? Also, difference images in Fig. 4 would make it easier to recognize where the proposed model deviates from the target. In 3.1, the authors state: “This means that the two metrics represent the superiority of DeepCVR to the DIP-based method”. This statement is wrong. As the DIP based method is the target, the metric can only measure the alignment between prediction and target, but not superiority. The phrasing of the abstract is somewhat clunky and not easy to understand, e.g., “Therefore, the use of the 3D volumes enables to achieve”, or “Here, there is a Deep Image Prior Method”. This should be revisited to state the problem statement and approach more clearly.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The methodological details and network architectures are comprehensively and clearly described throughout the paper, which facilitates the reproducibility of the proposed approach. 2.The authors explicitly discuss the computational efficiency and time-cost advantages of the algorithm. This significant reduction in inference time highlights the method’s potential for real-world deployment and clinical translation.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The manuscript requires proofreading to improve its academic tone and formatting. There are instances of colloquial phrasing and obvious grammatical errors, such as the sentence: “Also, the multi-focus image sequence be obtained using the microscope without additional hardware modifications.” These issues should be carefully corrected. 2.Figure 2 lacks an explicit representation of the latent variable s_{3D}, which is discussed in the main text. The figure should be updated to include this annotation for better alignment with the text. 3.The objectivity of the experimental setup is flawed due to a circular dependency in data generation. According to the manuscript, the 3D cell volumes (ground truth) used for training and validating DeepCVR are generated by the DIP-based method. However, the DIP-based method simultaneously serves as the primary baseline for evaluation. This compromises the fairness of the experiments. Ideally, the authors should utilize open-source datasets with established gold standards. In the absence of available objective datasets, ground truths should be simulated using physical models or independently validated third-party methods rather than the baseline method itself. 4.In the experimental section, critical evaluation metrics (PSNR and SSIM) are “calculated by comparing the reconstructed volumes by DeepCVR and the DIP-based method.” Consequently, achieving high metric scores merely demonstrates that DeepCVR’s outputs closely approximate those of the DIP-based method. This mathematical proximity cannot substantiate claims regarding “the superiority of DeepCVR to the DIP-based method,” which further highlights the aforementioned flaw in the dataset construction. 5.Based on the current results, it is evident that DeepCVR achieves higher inference efficiency compared to the DIP-based method. However, there is a lack of valid numerical evidence to demonstrate a distinct advantage in reconstruction performance. If the primary objective of this paper is solely to demonstrate that DeepCVR accelerates inference while strictly maintaining the performance of the DIP-based method, the manuscript’s claims must be revised to accurately reflect and emphasize this specific contribution. Conversely, if the authors intend to claim superior reconstruction performance, they must include additional baseline comparisons (beyond the DIP-based method) or revise the dataset and metric calculation methods to genuinely highlight DeepCVR’s performance improvements.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We address the major concerns below. (1) Justification for VAE + Teacher-Student over End-to-End U-Net (R2, Meta) Our study faces a large cross-modality domain gap between 2D multi-focus images (input) and 3D volumes (output), with limited training data (see (4)). A direct end-to-end model therefore needs to simultaneously learn both cross-modal mapping and 3D volume reconstruction under these constraints. Our strategy for addressing this challenge is to decompose it into two simpler tasks. First, CellVAE (teacher) learns both the latent representation (z_3D) and intermediate features (s_3D) from 3D volumes alone. Second, MF-CellEncoder (student) aligns these intermediate and latent representations. This decomposition is motivated by cross-modal knowledge distillation in [15]. A direct end-to-end U-Net comparison would be a valuable future extension. (2) Why a Probabilistic VAE for Deterministic Reconstruction? / Skip Connections (R2, Meta) During inference, we use the deterministic mean representation μ_MF directly without sampling. The probabilistic formulation is used only during training to regularize the latent space and encourage a smooth and structured representation, facilitating cross-modal alignment through the distillation loss in Eq. 3.Regarding the skip connections, these pathways pass intermediate features s_3D, explicitly aligned with MF-CellEncoder through the third term of Eq. 3, following intermediate-representation distillation in [15]. Without these skip features, the distillation would rely primarily on z_3D. In this case, DeepCVR would potentially lose spatial information critical for high-fidelity decoding. (3) Circular Dependency: DIP as Both Training Target and Baseline (R4, R2, Meta) We acknowledge this limitation. The primary contribution of DeepCVR is to achieve approximately 1.1x10^4 speedup while maintaining reconstruction quality comparable to DIP. However, there is no publicly available ground-truth 3D dataset for bright-field multi-focus cell reconstruction. Therefore, we use DIP-reconstructed volumes based on physical imaging models in [2,13] as the best available pseudo-ground truth. We will revise all related claims, including the imprecise phrase “superiority of DeepCVR to the DIP-based method” in Section 3.1, to accurately reflect this contribution. (4) Train/Test Split Not Specified (R2) We did not use all 320 samples as training data. All samples were split randomly into 80% training (256 samples), 10% validation (32 samples), and 10% test (32 samples). The metrics in Table 1 were computed exclusively on the test set. We will explicitly state this split in the revision to prevent misinterpretation. (5) Blurriness and Latent Space Effectiveness (R1) The consistently high PSNR (avg. 42.99 dB) and SSIM (avg. 0.9974) on the test set indicate that the distillation successfully transfers both intermediate features and latent representations from CellVAE to MF-CellEncoder. The observed blurring is an inherent characteristic of VAE-based smooth latent regularization, as acknowledged in Section 3.3.Per-dimension KL divergence analysis to further characterize posterior behavior would be a valuable future direction. [Minor Points] (R1, R4) (a) The classification of NILM, LSIL, HSIL, and SCC is based on the Bethesda System. (b) We will annotate s_3D and z_3D in Fig. 2.(c) We will clarify that the padded 12th z-slice is discarded prior to loss computation. (d) Fig. 4 shows the reconstructed 3D volumes in which the color of each voxel is determined by its transmittance value, while Fig. 5 shows the grayscale multi-focus images simulated via [13]. We will clarify this in the revision. (e) We will also correct all grammatical errors noted by R2 and R4.(f) Upon acceptance, we will release our code publicly. As our data consists of internal clinical data, public release is not possible.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper addresses the problem of 3D volume reconstruction from multi-focus images with the goal of speeding up the reconstruction. The proposed model builds on the Deep Image Prior (DIP), here combined with a teacher-student distillation approach to process cross-modal data. The three reviewers highlight the clarity of the exposed method and the important reduction in computational time. The main raised drawback is the lack of justification for such a complex pipeline (R2): why teacher-student distillation instead of, for instance, an end-to-end U-Net? (not compared to), why a probabilistic model if reconstruction is deterministic and does not need sampling? How to justify the use of skip connections in a VAE architecture? Another important issue is the potential lack of objectivity in the experimental setup (R2, R4), given that DIP is used for training and is thus considered the target. As a result, the current PSNR and SSIM scores cannot support the claim that DeepCVR performs better than DIP (other than in speed), calling for a revision of the claims. In addition, R1 and R2 note that the reconstructed volumes are blurry. Also, R2 suggests better describing the dataset and experimental setup (train/test sets), the metrics used, and discussing whether the achieved performance deviations are relevant in practice. Finally, although overall the paper was considered clear and reproducible from the explanations, several clarification remarks were made regarding the effective use of latent variables (R1), the treatment of the padded slices in the downstream task (R1), and a need for proofreading (R2 & R4), | This paper remains borderline after the clarifications of rebuttal. While R1 and R4 support acceptance focusing on the obtained speedup. R2 advocates for rejection, given the lack of comparison to a straightforward baseline to justify the complexity of the proposed approach, and the reliance on another algorithm DIP used both as target and a baseline (given there is no ground truth at the moment). Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviews remain somewhat mixed. R2 is still not fully satisfied with the revision and maintains a recommendation of reject. However, the majority of the reviewers view the revision positively and consider that the authors have adequately addressed the main concerns. Taking the overall discussion into account, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend acceptance as the authors have addressed the main concerns about the latent space design, the motivation for the architecture, and the interpretation of the evaluation. The rebuttal also clarified that the core contribution is the large speedup over DIP while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality. Although minor methodological questions and inextensive experimental varidations remain, they were sufficiently clarified for a positive final judgment, and the overall post-rebuttal feedback supports acceptance.

title: FreeBridge: Variational Schrödinger Bridges for Cellular Transition Dynamics
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The authors tackle an interesting problem, namely modeling single-cell state transitions using generative models, which has several applications in biology. 2.The authors introduce a novel loss function to constrain the cellular manifold, in contrast to previous works. 3.Overall, the paper is well written and easy to follow.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The Schrödinger bridge problem is not introduced with sufficient clarity, and there are several inconsistencies in the notation and equations. 2.Equation (3) corresponds to the forward diffusion process used in standard diffusion models. It is unclear how the proposed approach differs from or extends existing diffusion-based methods. 3.Equation (2), the construction of the support bank is not clearly explained. 4.It is unclear how the authors assess trajectory consistency, given that intermediate states are not available in the data. 5.The numerical approximation of the loss function is not clearly described. 6.The paper does not specify the architecture of the neural networks used, nor does it provide sufficient training details. 7.The qualitative evaluation is limited, relying on only two images. It would be beneficial to include visualizations of intermediate states, as modeling such states is a central objective of the work.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1) The introduction provides a well-structured motivation, correctly identifying that because infinitely many stochastic processes can connect identical marginals, endpoint alignment does not determine intermediate evolution. 2) The most compelling contribution is the Empirical Latent Support Regularization, which addresses a key limitation of standard generative models that often produce shortest-path trajectories. By penalizing transitions that enter non-biological voids, FreeBridge represents a significant advancement toward achieving realistic in silico virtual cell simulations. 3) The Cell Engine formulation, which decouples the State Unit from the Transition Rule, offers a highly effective and modular architectural design. This separation ensures that the underlying definition of a cellular state remains stable while learning complex transport dynamics. Furthermore, Figure 1 is excellently designed, providing a clear and accessible overview of the entire framework. 4) A critical technical contribution is the implementation of a nearest-neighbor-based support cost to regularize intermediate states. This effectively penalizes trajectories traversing regions of the latent space unsupported by observed morphologies, solving the problem of stochastic processes connecting endpoints through biologically implausible states. Figure 2 is instrumental in building intuition for this mechanism, while the results in Table 2 and Figure 4 provide empirical evidence regarding the necessity of the support bank. 5) Through extensive benchmarking in Table 1, the authors demonstrate that FreeBridge consistently outperforms recent distribution-alignment baselines, including PhenDiff, IMPA, and CellFlux, across three major datasets: BBBC021, RxRx1, and JUMP. The method achieves superior endpoint fidelity, as measured by FID and KID, while simultaneously yielding a significant reduction in intermediate support violations. 6) The qualitative samples presented in Figure 3 are highly persuasive, demonstrating the model’s ability to preserve compound-specific morphological structures with high fidelity.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1) Implementation details are significantly underspecified, hindering the reproducibility of the work. Given the space constraints of the submission template, the release of open-source code is essential to make the framework fully replicable. Specifically, the manuscript does not disclose the architecture or pre-training regime of the frozen encoder used within the State Unit, nor does it specify the dimensionality of the resulting feature embeddings. Furthermore, the architecture of the FreeBridge model itself remains unknown; while Figure 3 displays generated images, the necessary decoder components are not described in the text. 2) While the fixed geometry strategy is conceptually elegant, the transition rule is entirely dependent on the fidelity of the frozen encoder. If this encoder fails to capture subtle but biologically critical morphological features during its initial training, the subsequent Schrödinger Bridge transport will be fundamentally constrained to a sub-optimal manifold that cannot be corrected during the transition learning phase. 3) As the paper acknowledges that true single-cell trajectories are unobservable due to chemical fixation, the evaluation of trajectory consistency relies heavily on the Support Violation Rate. While this metric confirms that intermediate states align with known cellular morphologies, it does not strictly prove that the learned sequence of states is biologically accurate, only that it is realistic according to the empirical bank. 4) Although the authors utilize a minibatch approximation to mitigate the computational cost of calculating the empirical support distance, the approach still requires B x B distance comparisons at every discretization step. For high-dimensional embeddings or larger batch sizes, this requirement could significantly impact training efficiency compared to unconstrained generative models.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Well written. The path constraint based on empirical data is an interesting approach. The manuscript is well written and the key ideas are clearly explained.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Code not provided
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and the Area Chair. We use this response to clarify the theoretical framing, which addresses several of R1’s concerns, and to outline camera-ready revisions for the reproducibility issues raised across reviews. Theoretical framing and relation to diffusion (R1.W1, W2, W5) We agree the Schrödinger Bridge positioning was not stated clearly enough. Eq. (3) specifies the controlled SDE for the candidate path measure, using a Brownian noising process as reference. While this resembles the forward process in diffusion models, FreeBridge does not learn a singlemarginal diffusion score; instead, it optimizes a bridge path measure with fixed initial and terminal marginal constraints and an empirical state cost. Eq. (9) can be written as a Generalized Schrödinger Bridge objective with state cost Vt(z) = λdemp(z)2, where demp is the nearest-neighbor distance to the observed cellular morphology support. The camera-ready will make this GSB positioning explicit, add the GSBM reference, and correct notation inconsistencies in Sec. 2.We will also clarify the previously imprecise statement on underdetermination: (i) endpoint-only marginal matching is underdetermined before specifying a reference process; (ii) classical SB is well-defined once a Brownian reference is fixed; (iii) FreeBridge augments this with a data-driven state cost anchoring intermediate paths to the empirical manifold. Support bank and numerical approximation (R1.W3, W5) We will distinguish the population-level support in Eq. (2) from the minibatch estimator used in training, in which demp is computed against the union of control and perturbed embeddings in the current batch — a stochastic minibatch approximation to the population state-cost term under i.i.d. sampling. The camera-ready will provide the full discrete-time estimator, including time discretization, nearest-neighbor computation, normalization, and which quantities receive gradients. Trajectory evaluation and qualitative results (R1.W4, W7, R2.W3) Because fixed-cell assays do not provide observed single-cell trajectories, true temporal ordering cannot be directly verified. The Support Violation Rate measures whether intermediate states remain within the empirical morphology manifold — a support-feasibility metric, not a direct proof of biological temporal correctness. On this metric, endpoint-only baselines perform worse than FreeBridge (Table 1: Rviol = 0.11 for FreeBridge vs 0.31 for the strongest baseline; lower is better). Wewill state this limitation explicitly and retain the Mechanism-of-Action ablation (Table 3: 72.08% full model vs 65.08% without geometric regularization) as an orthogonal evaluation independent of the support-violation metric. The camera-ready will also include intermediate-state visualizations beyond endpoint samples. Implementation and reproducibility (R1.W6, R2.W1, R3.W1) We agree key implementation details were underspecified. The camera-ready supplementary will include a full appendix covering the frozen encoder architecture and pretraining, embedding dimensionality, drift network, decoder used in Fig. 3, discretization scheme, hyperparameters, batch sizes, random seeds, and evaluation protocol. Source code and checkpoints will be released upon publication Frozen-encoder limitation and computational cost (R2.W2, W4) We acknowledge the Cell Engine design fixes the latent geometry through a frozen encoder, so features absent from its pretraining cannot be recovered by transport learning alone. The B × B support-distance computation uses batched torch.cdist; this does not remove the O(B2) scaling but reduces constant factors. The camera-ready will report measured wall-clock and memory at the batch sizes used. We thank R2 and R3 for the supportive assessments and R1 for the careful critique. These clarifications will be incorporated into the camera-ready to improve clarity, reproducibility, and theoretical positioning.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): There are strong discrepancies among the three reviewers, consisting of one reject and two accept. The paper tackles an important task of modelling single cell state transitions, for which FreeBridge, a constrained diffusion and transport framework is proposed, with favorable empirical results. Meanwhile, there are a number of aspects of the work that raise concerns. It would be beneficial if the authors provide further input and clarifications in the areas specifically brought out by the reviewers, including but not limited to, Schrödinger bridge problem; theoretical justifications and analyses; implementation details such as details of the engaged NNs, training details, and reproducibility; empirical evaluations esp. qualitative results; the computational cost of nearest-neighbor check.

title: INST-Align: Implicit Neural Alignment for Spatial Transcriptomics via Canonical Expression Fields
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Although INST-Align is optimized for alignment (embedding quality is a byproduct rather than the primary target), it still produces spatial embeddings that are useful for clustering analysis. 2.The Spatial Expression Alignment Loss and Jacobian Regularization are biologically motivated and reasonably designed.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The abstract claims state-of-the-art performance, but the results are not consistently strong across all datasets (e. g. , D1 and D2), where existing methods remain competitive or superior. A more balanced discussion and analysis of these cases would strengthen the paper. 2.It is not clearly specified whether all baselines use the same preprocessing (e. g. , adaptive ICP) and data splits. In addition, key hyperparameters (e. g. , in Eq. (6) and (8)) are fixed without sensitivity analysis, raising concerns about robustness and reproducibility. 3.The ablation does not fully disentangle the contributions of individual components, particularly the loss terms in Phase 2 (e. g. , L_recon vs. L_match). Moreover, it is conducted on a single dataset, which limits its generality. 4.While the method is designed to jointly perform alignment and integration, the results suggest that improvements are uneven. In particular, Phase 1 mainly enhances embedding quality, while its impact on alignment metrics is less evident, weakening the claim of strong mutual benefit. 5.Although the method achieves favorable average performance, improvements are not consistently dominant across datasets or metrics. For example, gains in Chamfer distance are not always matched by comparable improvements in OT or NN accuracy, making the practical advantage less clear.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper is motivated by a real and important problem. Multi-slice spatial transcriptomics alignment remains a challenging. The paper’s motivation for coupling geometric alignment with expression-level information is logical and broadly consistent with recent reviews and benchmarking studies in ST. 2.The proposed combination of a shared canonical field and coordinate deformation is novel and technically reasonable. 3.The model architecture is clearly presented. The two-stage fitting (pretraining and joint training of deformation and canonical consistency) is well established and logically organized. 4.The method is evaluated on diverse spatial transcriptomics datasets, and the paper reports multiple alignment metrics, including OT Accuracy, NN Accuracy, and Chamfer distance. In addition, the authors provide a downstream evaluation of biological embedding quality.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The experimental gains are somewhat uneven, and the biological validity of the learned embeddings remains under-validated. Some performance variation is expected given the noisy and unsupervised nature of spatial transcriptomics alignment. However, the downstream analysis in Table 2 shows that INST-Align does not achieve SOTA embedding quality, which weakens the strength of the claimed “joint alignment and integration” formulation. This cannot be fully dismissed as a mere “byproduct”, since the paper emphasizes biologically meaningful embeddings, and getting a good embedding is the final touch to a scientific analysis. 2.The manuscript does not provide clustering visualizations. Although the paper includes a 3D reconstruction example on DLPFC, the visualization is shown only with ground-truth labels, and DLPFC itself exhibits relatively limited slice-wise deformation, making this example less compelling as evidence for the claimed advantages. 3.The central methodology is not fully analyzed. The manuscript does not provide a direct analysis of how the shared canonical field mitigates batch effects, nor does it isolate the contribution of the proposed Spatial-Expression Alignment Loss in the ablation study. This is important because recent benchmarking work suggests that multi-slice ST performance is highly context dependent and that alignment and integration quality should be dissected carefully. 4.Implementation details and computational cost are insufficiently reported. This is a concern because the full training pipeline requires 700 epochs in total (300 + 400), which is difficult to judge the practical efficiency of the proposed method relative to competing alignment approaches.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Accurate reconstruction of coherent 3D tissue volumes from serial sections is a critical challenge, as slices undergo complex non-rigid distortions such as tearing and folding during sample preparation. However, existing alignment methods often treat alignment and integration as independent steps. Relying on integration-based methods risks over-correcting and diminishing genuine biological diversity, while geometric methods lack expression-level feedback. Furthermore, biological complexity makes ground-truth correspondences largely unattainable, raising the need for a robust unsupervised strategy. To overcome these limitations, the authors design INST-Align, which employs a two-phase training strategy to establish a stable canonical embedding space before jointly optimizing deformation and spatial-feature matching. Furthermore, the proposed spatial-expression alignment loss combines geometric proximity and canonical-field feature similarity to drive unsupervised non-rigid registration. This design aims to turn alignment into a mutually constrained reconstruction task.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The integration of a deformation network with a shared canonical field represents a highly promising and valuable approach for ST multi-slice alignment. To further elevate the clarity and impact of this strong manuscript, the authors might consider clarifying a few methodological details: 1.The use of an asymmetric weighting scheme in the Jacobian regularization to penalize tissue compression more heavily than expansion is an intuitive and physically plausible design choice. However, since the specific weights chosen directly impact the smoothness of the displacement field, their specific values could benefit from a bit more validation. The paper would be further strengthened if the authors could provide a brief ablation study or visualize the resulting vector fields under different weight settings. This would beautifully illustrate that they indeed preserve biologically plausible cell densities without introducing artifacts. 2.The claim that the spatial-expression alignment loss utilizes an adaptive temperature and EMA scale factors is compelling. While the current two-phase training is a solid baseline, the interpretability of this dynamic matching could be made even more convincing. The authors might consider visualizing the convergence curves of these dynamic scaling factors during the joint optimization phase. Showing that these parameters stabilize naturally over the 400 epochs would wonderfully solidify the paper’s core contribution regarding optimization stability. 3.The model achieves impressive state-of-the-art results across most datasets, particularly in Chamfer distance reduction on large-deformation sections. However, to provide a more comprehensive evaluation, it would be valuable to briefly discuss the potential for error accumulation when performing 3D tissue reconstructions from consecutively aligned slices. Including a short discussion in the conclusion regarding how the current pairwise framework might be extended to include a global multi-slice consistency objective would provide readers with a more objective understanding of the model’s limitations and future scalability. 4.The biologically meaningful embeddings generated by INST-Align are one of its strongest aspects. There is, however, a minor area for expansion regarding the biological validation, which is currently limited to clustering-based metrics like ARI and NMI. Could the authors kindly clarify or evaluate how these embeddings perform on specific spatial trajectory inference tasks or continuous phenotype mappings? Detailing this downstream utility would greatly help readers fully understand the mechanics and ensure the biological relevance of the canonical field.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and MR. All numbers below are from the submitted manuscript or characterizations of the submitted runs. 1.SOTA claim [R1.1, R1.5, R2.1, MR-1]. The claim is best mean across nine datasets. On D1/D2, top methods differ by at most 0.037 OT and 0.031 NN; on D3 we lead OT (.839) and NN (.849). The advantage is decisive under large deformations: Chamfer 12.6/17.1/11.9 on MB2/MB11/ME vs. 166.2/103.3/12.0 (Spateo) and 173.1/51.7/235.5 (PASTE). Mean OT .702, NN .719, Chamfer 22.6 are best across all baselines. The abstract phrase “the strongest baseline” will be replaced with “PASTE”, consistent with §3.2 and Conclusion. 2.Why paired-then-canonical [R2.Q1, MR-2]. A reference-only ExprINR would bake the reference’s batch signature into the canonical signal; deformation would then drag the source onto reference-specific artifacts. Phase 1’s two ExprINRs share one decoder (§2.2): the decoder must reconstruct both slices from coordinates alone, forcing slice-specific noise into the reconstruction residual and out of the canonical embedding. This is the integration step. The source INR is discardable in Phase 2 because the deformation network maps source coordinates into the canonical frame, where one shared field suffices. The design is the explicit mechanism behind “joint alignment+integration”, not redundant scaffolding. 3.Component isolation [R1.3, R2.3, R3.1, MR-2]. Table 3 dissociates three orthogonal axes: removing Phase 1 collapses embedding (ARI .334->.045) with alignment intact (OT .810->.813); removing Phase 2 degrades alignment (Chamfer .36->.56); removing Jacobian degrades both (Chamfer .49, ARI .287). The Phase-1 ablation pattern reproduces on MouseEmbryo (OT .75->.69, ARI .22->.13), confirming the trend is not dataset-specific. 4.Cost and reproducibility [R1.2, R2.Q3, MR-4]. On MouseEmbryo (~37k cells, single RTX 5080 16GB) INST-Align trains in 95 s – faster than PASTE (232 s) and STalign (435 s), competitive with Spateo. The 300+400-epoch schedule is dataset-agnostic and runs on consumer hardware. All datasets use the identical Dong et al. [11] pipeline; baselines run released code under default init. Core design is fixed across all nine datasets – two-phase training, shared canonical field, spatial-expression matcher, 5:1 Jacobian asymmetry. Only scale/geometry settings vary, and were fixed before final evaluation: robustness in the architecture, not missing sensitivity. 5.Specific items. R2.Q2 (ICP). Rigid ICP removes only translation/rotation; the residual in Fig. 2(a) is exactly the tearing/folding the non-rigid step corrects – expected, not failure. R3.1 (Jacobian). The 5x compression penalty follows the local-invertibility argument of [29]: near-singular compression destroys the diffeomorphism, expansion does not. Table 3’s “w/o Jacobian” row quantifies the effect. R3.2 (tau / scales). In the submitted runs, tau, s_sp, s_ft stabilize within 0-25, 0-10, 12-65 epochs across all datasets – natural early self-calibration. R3.3 (drift). Acknowledged as a current limitation in the Conclusion. R2 / R3.4 (biology). The canonical field is coordinate-conditioned and differentiable; trajectory inference and continuous phenotype mapping are downstream uses of the same trained model , not separate methodology – consistent with Table 2, where our embeddings beat PCA and Seurat despite alignment being primary. Closing. Each MR ask – inconsistent gains, isolation of contributions, utility of embeddings, reproducibility – is answered from the submitted Tables 1-3 plus characterizations of the submitted runs, in compliance with rebuttal policy. R1 already recommended Accept (5, very confident). R2’s Q1/Q2/Q3 are addressed in §2/§5/§4 and R3’s asks in §3/§5; on R2’s own terms (“open to raising my score to 4 or 5”), we ask R2 and R3 to update their scores.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): It is an interesting paper that presents an important problem and proposes a coherent method with a novel coupling between non-rigid deformation and a shared canonical expression field. However, the results do not quite convincingly support the claims. The performance gains are inconsistent across datasets and metrics. It is unclear how much of the gain results from joint alignment and integration, especially from using a shared canonical field and spatial-expression alignment loss. We believe that more experiments are needed to better demonstrate the utility of the learned embeddings. Reproducibility needs more information such as fairness of preprocessing, the sensitivity to hyper-parameters, the run time, and any other relevant information for replicating the experiments. Please carefully address these points with clear evidence and additional ablations/analyses, and make the manuscript more balanced. | After rebuttal, R1 maintains Accept after the clarifications on design, ablations, cost, and reproducibility, while R2 raises the score to Accept after the authors addressed concerns about pre-ICP, canonical space, and experimental interpretation. R3 originally rates weak reject but did not submit final rating. After review, I think the concerns would not block this paper. I vote for acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This work proposes a registration approach for spatial transcriptomics from different sections. The developed approach makes use of implicit neural representations to model the spatial deformation as well as mRNA expression. While there was mixed review enthusiasm before the rebuttal, reviewer sentiment was largely positive after the rebuttal. Reviewers appreciated the tackled problem and the average gains obtained by the proposed method compared to competing approaches. There are some remaining concerns regarding the quality of the obtained joint embeddings (as performance is lower than for specialized methods) and the ability of the approach to extend to multi slice alignment (the dreaded banana effect comes to mind for 3D reconstructions from pairwise 2D registration) but overall this paper provides an interesting approach for a challenging task. Hence, in my opinion, it is suitable for presentation at MICCAI. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers generally agreed that the paper addresses an important problem and introduces a novel framework that jointly models spatial alignment and expression integration through a shared Canonical Expression Field. Although concerns were initially raised regarding the consistency of performance gains, component attribution, biological validation, and reproducibility, the rebuttal provided satisfactory clarifications grounded in the submitted manuscript, leading both initially borderline reviewers to raise their final recommendations to Accept. Given the methodological novelty, strong overall experimental performance, and positive post-rebuttal consensus, I recommend acceptance.

title: Inverse Protocol Prediction from Spheroid Microscopy Imaging via Morphology-Aware Structured Learning
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) The paper introduces a novel problem formulation and new research direction for spheroid image analysis. Additionally, the paper demonstrates the feasibility of this direction through a comprehensive empirical study. 2) The paper introduces a custom deep learning (DL) network for mitigating acquisition bias.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) The motivation for the proposed task is not adequately established in the introduction. The paper argues that protocol or metadata inconsistencies may remain undetected and affect reproducibility; however, in curated experimental datasets, metadata (cell line, media, seeding density, imaging setup) are explicitly recorded. 2) The paper lacks a dedicated methodology section, with the proposed framework primarily described through a high-level figure (Fig. 1) and scattered implementation details. Critical components such as the morphometry–vision fusion mechanism and the hierarchical multi-task transformer (HMTT) are not formally defined (no mathematical formulation, or architectural specification). 3) The paper addresses acquisition bias through a custom DL framework. However, the effectiveness of this strategy is evaluated using only a single model configuration, without comparison to alternative architectures or bias-mitigation techniques.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The approach is novel and addresses an existing need - there is limited prior research on the topic of inverse protocol prediction in general. In addition to the listed application areas of reproducibility auditing and protocol validation, the work has potential in data standardization in gathering large biomedical image datasets from different sources. The methods applied seem appropriate for the aims of the study, and use is generally well justified. The authors have taken steps towards reducing bias in gathering the datasets by performing ablation studies and cross-data set validation, among others.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The impact of the study is limited by focusing on cross-replicate generalization rather than showing the robustness of the method – with timepoints being the only measure with held-out test classes (2 out of 109 classes). For the timepoints, a more modest prediction (F1 score of 0.75) was achieved. To my understanding, the paper does not disclose the accuracy of the model in predicting the held-out classes – this would be of interest due to being both the metric with the lowest accuracy and with held-out classes. To me, it would be intuitive to consider image intensity and contrast measures to be metrics that could inadvertently point the network to lean towards microscopy images taken in a specific study and introduce bias that way. If I have understood correctly, withholding images with a differing intensity spectrum could reveal how much the network relies on these factors instead of the textures.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Predicting protocol metadata from spheroid morphology is a well-motivated problem for reproducibility auditing and quality control in high-throughput 3D culture experiments. The experimental split by technical replicate is a strong design choice and is more credible than random image-level splitting for this problem. It reduces the risk of obvious leakage across acquisition sessions. The empirical study is broad with multiple segmentation models benchmarked and several IPP architectures are compared including convolutional, transformer, hybrid, fusion-based, and hierarchical variants. The manuscript includes useful per-label analysis showing which protocol variables are strongly versus weakly recoverable from morphology. The biological-only evaluation is a thoughtful addition because it attempts to separate biologically meaningful prediction from acquisition-driven variables. The interpretability analysis is relevant and practically useful. The paper does not just chase high accuracy, but also tries to assess whether predictions are based on plausible biological cues versus technical confounders. The overall practical framing is strong. Even if novelty at the module level is moderate, the task formulation and benchmarking package could be valuable.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: HMTT is positioned as a key contribution but it is not the best-performing model in the main table, and the paper does not clearly show that hierarchical conditioning improves joint protocol consistency over simpler structured baselines. The paper should clearly explain whether uncertainty is computed across seeds and how confidence intervals were derived. reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the novelty of the IPP task, replicate-aware evaluation protocol, and biological interpretability analysis. We address the main concerns below. Motivation and practical relevance of IPP: IPP is not intended to replace recorded metadata, but rather to serve as a complementary auditing framework for detecting protocol drift, incomplete/non-standardized annotations, acquisition inconsistencies, and cross-site variability in large microscopy workflows. Importantly, the biological-only evaluation (excluding microscope, magnification, and replicate variables) still achieves Biological Macro-F1=0.914, supporting that IPP captures biologically meaningful morphology-protocol associations rather than only acquisition artifacts. Methodology and HMTT clarification: We agree that additional formalization would improve clarity. Due to space constraints, some implementation details were condensed. The submitted pipeline trains RefineNet for binary segmentation and freezes it before IPP training; morphometrics are computed only from predicted masks, avoiding annotation leakage. For multimodal fusion, the image encoder produces visual embeddings (z_img = f_θ(x)), while normalized morphometric descriptors (m ∈ R^d) are projected as shape tokens and fused through a Transformer encoder before per-attribute prediction heads. HMTT factorizes inference as (P(y₁,…,y_K | x) = ∏ₖ P(yₖ | x, y_<k)), using teacher forcing during training and autoregressive decoding during inference. Domain-adversarial training optimizes (L_total = L_bio+L_domain) using a gradient reversal layer. Importantly, HMTT is not intended as the sole primary contribution or necessarily the best-performing architecture. Rather, the paper systematically evaluates convolutional, transformer, hybrid, fusion-based, and dependency-aware approaches to study the role of inductive bias, explicit morphometric priors, and label-structure modeling in IPP. Acquisition bias and robustness: Acquisition confounding is addressed through: (i) replicate-exclusive splitting; (ii) biological-only IPP excluding acquisition/replicate labels; and (iii) domain-adversarial training with replicate identity treated as domain. Grad-CAM further shows that biological predictions focus on spheroid morphology (boundary, compactness, internal organization), whereas replicate-related predictions exhibit diffuse/background attention patterns. We agree that an explicit intensity-spectrum holdout would provide an additional stress test and acknowledge this as a future direction. Held-out classes and robustness clarification: Results are reported on held-out technical replicates rather than random image splits. For 7/8 attributes, all validation/test classes appear during training; only timepoint includes two unseen test-only classes (000h and 032h), which are included in Table 4 evaluation. The lower timepoint F1 reflects gradual and overlapping morphological transitions rather than framework failure. Robustness is further supported by zero-shot transfer to RxRx1, where Image-Shape Fusion achieves F1=0.768 despite substantial modality/acquisition shift. Confidence intervals and reproducibility: Table 3 reports mean ± SD across three independent seeds (42,123,999), with 95% confidence intervals computed as (1.96×SD / √3). Segmentation and RxRx1 confidence intervals were computed analogously over evaluation samples. We acknowledge this could have been clearer. Code and implementation details will be released upon publication to support reproducibility. We thank the reviewers for the thoughtful feedback. We believe the discussion clarifies that the primary contribution is the introduction of IPP as a structured inference problem together with a replicate-aware benchmarking framework for studying biological and acquisition-related morphology signatures. We will address these clarity issues in the permitted minor revision.
