title: Non-parametric Prototypes Enable Semantic Graph Learning for Whole-Slide Pathology
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper constructs dataset-level non-parametric prototypes through a two-stage K-means clustering across WSIs, extending visual diversity modeling from individual slides to the dataset level; this design approach demonstrates significant relevance to the WSI classification task. The paper expands coarse-grained attribute text into fine-grained hierarchical text with three intensity levels, using prototypes as a bridge to calibrate the semantic affinity matrix between patches and text. By explicitly injecting hierarchical semantic information into the graph construction process, this coarse-to-fine multimodal alignment design distinguishes itself from mainstream direct-alignment methods.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper relies on K-means clustering for dataset-level prototype generation, yet it fails to discuss the sensitivity of the prototype count across datasets of varying scales or the criteria for its selection, leaving both reproducibility and generalization in doubt. The paper generates hierarchical attribute text using GPT-5.2 followed by manual review, but it does not report the evaluation metrics or criteria for text quality. Furthermore, the impact of text content on final classification performance lacks targeted ablation, leaving the relationship between text quality and model performance unclear.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Novel use of non-parametric prototypes: The paper introduces dataset-level non-parametric prototypes that capture global visual diversity across WSIs, which is more expressive than conventional instance-level patch selection and helps improve generalization. Effective integration of multimodal information: The method combines visual features with both coarse- and fine-grained pathological attribute texts, and further models their hierarchical relationships, leading to better visual–semantic alignment than standard fusion approaches. Prototype-guided graph learning design: The proposed semantic calibration and graph learning module leverages prototypes to refine inter-patch relationships beyond simple spatial adjacency, which is a meaningful extension of graph-based WSI modeling.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Reliance on generated textual descriptions: The attribute texts are generated (e.g., via GPT-based tools) and manually refined, which may introduce bias or inconsistency. The robustness of the method to different or noisy textual descriptions is not thoroughly analyzed. Limited clinical validation: Although the method is evaluated on multiple datasets, including a private one, the evaluation focuses on classification metrics without demonstrating clinical utility (e.g., impact on diagnosis, interpretability for pathologists). Evaluation limitations: The experiments are based on fixed data splits and lack more robust validation strategies such as cross-validation. Additionally, comparisons with more recent large-scale multimodal or foundation models are limited, making it harder to fully assess the competitiveness of the approach.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The proposed integration of visual prototypes with textual attributes (both coarse- and fine-grained) to construct a semantic graph is an interesting and well-motivated approach. It attempts to explicitly model dataset-level visual diversity and align it with hierarchical pathological descriptions, which effectively addresses the limitation of isolated patch-level processing in current WSI analysis. The hierarchical progression from patch selection to semantic graph construction forms a logically sound pipeline for vision-language fusion in pathology.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Despite the interesting design, there are critical ambiguities regarding the inference pipeline and the fairness of experimental comparisons that must be addressed: Unclear Testing/Inference Pipeline: The testing pipeline is not clearly described in the manuscript. It is difficult to understand the exact end-to-end inference procedure when a completely new, unseen WSI is fed into the network. Potential Label Leakage: It is unclear whether (and how) textual inputs are utilized during the testing phase. If the corresponding textual prompts are generated using ground-truth class names (or descriptions derived directly from the specific diagnosis) and fed into the model for inference, this would introduce severe label leakage. The authors must clarify the exact source and generation process of textual prompts during the testing phase to rule out this possibility. Unfair Baseline Comparison regarding LLM Backbones: In the experimental comparisons, the baseline method Ref [5] utilizes an LLM (GPT-4o mini), whereas this paper reportedly employs a different/upgraded LLM (“GPT-5.2”). This discrepancy raises a critical question: Could the performance gap between the proposed method and Ref [5] be primarily attributed to the superiority of the underlying LLM rather than the architectural design of ProtoSG-Net? To ensure a fair comparison, the authors should provide experimental evidence where the LLM used in Ref [5] is replaced with the exact same LLM used in their method.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers and the AC for constructive feedback. We will address the major concerns one by one. 1）@R1: ablation The sensitivity of the dataset-level prototypes have been studied in Section 3.3 and Fig. 4 (c). The optimal number of prototypes is 15 for 3 datasets, and the results fluctuate only slightly around this value, indicating low sensitivity to this hyperparameter. For reproducibility, dataset-level prototypes are obtained via standard K-means clustering, and all hyperparameters and experimental details are reported in Section 3.1, enabling straightforward replication. 2）@R1@R2: attribute text quality All attribute texts were reviewed by professional pathologists to check their quality without any modifications, so very few bias or inconsistency is introduced. Coarse-grained texts describe high-level pathological attributes (e.g., the overall differentiation and maturity of cells within the tissue) without defining“correct”values, and fine-grained texts simply expand these attributes into three intensity levels. We additionally conduct robustness experiments by adding Gaussian noise (mean=0, std=0.01, 0.1, 0.5) to textual features. The results show that model performance remains stable (e.g., Acc and F1 vary within 2% on all datasets), indicating insensitivity to minor variations in text content. For instance, on TCGA-NSCLC, acc stays at 96.65% across different noise levels. 3）@R3: inference pipeline and label leakage clarification During testing, the dataset-level prototypes are not regenerated. Instead, the prototypes generated from the training set slides are directly used for patch selection, ensuring a fully end-to-end inference for a completely unseen case without any access to its label. Regarding textual inputs, all attribute texts describe visual properties of the tissue (e.g., the overall differentiation and maturity of cells within the tissue) and are initially coarse-grained, then expanded into fine-grained intensity levels (high, moderate, low), all of which are used as input. These texts contain no information derived from ground-truth class labels or patient diagnosis, eliminating any possibility of label leakage. 4）@R2: clinical validation The clinical relevance of the model is supported by attention visualization in Fig. 3 and Section 3.2, where the patches with the highest attention scores correspond to pathologically meaningful regions. These visualizations highlight that the model focuses on lesion areas, demonstrating interpretability and alignment with clinical expectations. 5）@R2: evaluation We conduct 5-fold cross-validation on Camelyon+ comparing our model with TransMIL (previous second-best). Our model outperforms it by 0.42% in Acc, 1.93% in F1, 0.11% in AUROC, and 3.54% in PRAUC. We also conduct zero-shot classification on two large-scale multimodal foundation models: PLIP (Acc: 56.74%, AUROC: 46.26%) and CONCH (Acc: 59.01%, AUROC: 57.41%) on Camelyon+. These additional results suggest that our method remains competitive under cross-validation and compares favorably with recent foundation models. 6）@R3: fairness check for LLM backbone EmmPD’s metrics remain lower than ours across all three datasets with GPT-5.2-generated text (acc on TCGA-NSCLC: 94.74%; Placenta: 75.27%; Camelyon+: 87.59%). Besides, the LLM used in our study is indeed GPT-5.2, which was officially released in December 2025 and the latest available version at the time of our submission.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper is potentially acceptable. The methodological direction is relevant and moderately novel for MICCAI, especially in combining dataset-level prototypes with hierarchical semantic graph learning for WSI classification. The reported performance appears promising across multiple datasets. However, the current concerns are substantial and directly affect validity: possible label leakage during inference, unclear use and generation of text prompts at test time, unfair baseline comparison due to different LLM backbones, insufficient ablation of prototype/text/graph components, and weak reproducibility details. | Despite relying on some previously established components, the paper’s integration strategy provides a distinct, valuable, and proven contribution to multimodal and graph-based WSI classification. The robust experimental results firmly support its utility, making it a strong addition to the conference/journal. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes ProtoSG-Net, a prototype-guided semantic graph learning framework for whole slide image (WSI) classification that aims to better capture dataset-level visual diversity and improve multimodal alignment between visual features and pathological texts. Overall, the paper is interesting, technically sound, and addresses a relevant problem in computational pathology. After carefully considering the manuscript, the reviews, and the rebuttal, I find that the major concerns raised during the review process have been adequately addressed. In particular, the authors provided satisfactory clarifications regarding the use of GPT-5.2, the fairness of the corresponding comparisons, the quality of the generated attribute texts, and the inference procedure. These responses significantly improve confidence in both the methodology and the reported results. Therefore, I support acceptance of this paper at MICCAI. For the final version, I encourage the authors to incorporate the key clarifications provided in the rebuttal into the manuscript. In addition, Figure 2 could be further improved for readability. Specifically, the arrows and symbols in the green-highlighted region would benefit from more explicit explanations. The current depiction of the matrix multiplication operation is also somewhat confusing, particularly where two inputs are first merged by arrows before entering the matrix multiplication symbol. A clearer visual representation of the data flow and operations would substantially improve the accessibility of the method. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal sufficiently clarifies the inference pipeline, training-set prototype usage, and absence of label-derived textual prompts, which alleviates the most serious concern regarding potential label leakage. Although some concerns remain regarding text-quality dependence, robustness of the generated semantic attributes, and the reliance on additional rebuttal-only analyses, the prototype-guided semantic graph formulation is reasonably motivated and the post-rebuttal evidence places the paper marginally above the acceptance threshold.

title: POT-SAM3: Prompt-Only Tuning for One-Shot Electron Microscopy Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The problem tackled by this paper is practical and makes use of the general structure of workflows in EM. Weakly annotating a single slice and automatic dense prediction on future slices is a genuine improvement and speedup compared to traditional workflows. 2.The highly parameter-efficient formulation of the method where only concept tokens are learned and SAM3’s base weights are frozen is elegant. This avoids catastrophic forgetting and keeps compute low for large 3D volumes. 3.The inverse-warp consistency as a self-supervised proxy is a smart step to force robust tokens rather than memorization of a single labeled frame. 4.The new instance discovery on later frames is simple but effective in addressing a common failure mode of tracking-based propagation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Limited baseline comparison: The evaluation omits established EM-specific segmentation methods that represent current practice. Comparing primarily against general-purpose models (SAM2/3, PerSAM, HSNet) and a single supervised baseline (nnU-Net) makes it difficult to assess the method’s practical utility relative to domain-standard pipelines. 2.Ambiguous “one-shot” framing: The paper compares against HSNet as a “one-shot segmentation method” but the meaning of “one-shot” differs between methods. HSNet uses a support/query few-shot learning paradigm, while POT-SAM3 learns tokens from one annotated slice. This distinction should be clarified to avoid misleading comparisons. 3.nnU-Net comparison lacks clarity: The nnU-Net comparison is denoted as 10-shot. This should be explained more clearly. Does 10-shot refer to the nnU-Net learning from 10 fully annotated sections? The first 10 or any 10? Is it exposed to all volumes in the set? 4.An analysis of how performance degrades when instances split or merge across slices, which is a common issue in EM data, would strengthen the contribution.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper identifies the two real failure modes of vanilla SAM 3 on EM — concept mismatch and the need for per-frame prompts — and the proposed solution addresses both with a single mechanism. The motivation is well-articulated and the design follows directly from it. 2.Reproducibility is good. Hyperparameters are reported in detail (learning rate, schedule, NMS thresholds, novelty thresholds, training duration), and an anonymized code link is provided. 3.Surpassing 10-shot nnU-Net on Lucchi while using only first-frame supervision and updating <0.1% of parameters is a meaningful result, and the consistency across six tasks is reassuring. The improvement over vanilla SAM 3 (0.464 → 0.770 average Dice) is large and clearly attributable to the proposed adaptation.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Methodological novelty is limited. The core mechanism — learning a small set of prompt tokens while freezing the backbone — is a direct application of Visual Prompt Tuning (Jia et al., ECCV 2022, cited as [8]) to SAM 3.The novelty therefore lies in (a) initialization from box-derived prompt embeddings and (b) the auxiliary losses (inverse-warp consistency, token diversity). These are reasonable design choices but should be positioned more honestly as adaptation rather than a new paradigm. 2.Only Dice is reported, despite the paper framing the problem as instance segmentation. Standard instance metrics (AP at multiple IoU thresholds, panoptic quality, split/merge counts) are absent. This is a non-trivial gap because tracking-based methods can produce identity-consistent but topologically wrong masks that Dice cannot distinguish from correct ones. At minimum, AP@0.5 and AP@0.75 should be reported. 3.First-frame sensitivity is not analyzed. The entire approach hinges on the choice of the labeled section. If the first frame contains few or no instances of the target class, token learning degenerates. Reporting performance variance over different first-frame choices (e.g., 5 random selections per dataset) would substantially strengthen the empirical claims. 4.Lack of comparison with relevant SOTA results in the field. Although this paper uses few-shot segmentation, there are related works, and more comparisons should be made. 5.The “1000 epochs” training schedule for tuning three vectors per class on a single image deserves justification — this is a large compute budget for a “parameter-efficient” method, and the early-stopping behavior should be reported.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful low-annotation EM segmentation problem and proposes a workflow that is well aligned with serial-section data. The method is practical, parameter-efficient, and directly targets the need to reduce per-slice interaction during propagation. The empirical results are strong on the reported datasets. POT-SAM3 clearly improves over SAM3, SAM2, PerSAM, HSNet, and one-shot nnU-Net, and even surpasses 10-shot nnU-Net on the Lucchi sequences. This makes the paper practically interesting despite limited methodological novelty.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high. Prompt tuning, one-shot SAM personalization, and tracking-based propagation are all established directions, so the contribution is mainly a targeted adaptation of SAM3 to serial EM rather than a fundamentally new method. The evaluation remains limited in scale and detail. The number of sequences is small, robustness to different annotated slices is not tested, and the paper reports Dice only, without object-level or tracking-level metrics such as instance recall, ID consistency, or track fragmentation.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the AC and reviewers for the insightful feedback. We are glad they appreciated the practical value (R1,R2,R3), parameter-efficient design (R1,R2,R3), reproducibility (R2), and empirical effectiveness (R1,R2,R3) of our work. “Q” denotes the reviewer questions/weaknesses addressed below. Metrics (R1-Q4, R2-Q2, R3-Q2): We chose Dice as the primary metric to use a unified measure of final segmentation quality across different datasets. We agree that instance-level and tracking-level metrics would make the evaluation more complete. These metrics can in principle be computed from the existing predictions without additional experiments, and our checks show trends consistent with Dice. In accordance with the rebuttal guidelines, we cannot present detailed new quantitative results here; if permitted in the final revision, we will include more detailed metric reporting derived from the existing outputs. Fig. 2 provides a qualitative complement: under the same first-section supervision, POT-SAM3 produces more continuous masks that better match the target instances on frame 127, whereas the 10-shot nnU-Net reference shows more fragmented regions. While this cannot replace systematic instance- or tracking-level metrics, it still provides some indication of instance discovery and propagation quality. One-shot setting (R1-Q2, R1-Q3): All one-shot baselines use the same first fully annotated section. For HSNet, this section and its annotation form the support pair, and the remaining frames are queries. nnU-Net(10) is a stronger-supervision reference: for each task sequence, it is trained on 10 randomly sampled fully annotated images, yielding a separate model per task. By comparison, POT-SAM3 stores only three 256-D concept tokens per task, keeping the adaptation lightweight. First-frame sensitivity (R2-Q3): The intended workflow assumes that researchers select an initial section containing target instances. If this section is empty or highly unrepresentative, one-section adaptation becomes ill-posed; we will clarify this assumption and scope. EM-specific baseline (R1-Q1, R2-Q4): We agree that EM-specific methods are an important reference. However, these methods target different scenarios, such as fully supervised 3D segmentation, target-domain fine-tuning, or category-specific organelle models. Under our one-shot setting, directly comparable EM-specific baselines are rare, leaving this application scenario largely unexplored—this is one of the motivations for developing POT-SAM3.Forcing these methods into our one-shot setting would be unfair and would violate their original design assumptions, such as reliance on larger annotation budgets or complex 3D pipelines. Positioning (R2-Q1, R3-Q1): We did not intend to present POT-SAM3 as a new foundation model. Consistent with the manuscript, we position it as a parameter-efficient, low-interaction workflow for serial EM segmentation. Its contribution lies in adapting SAM3 to the one-section EM setting through concept-token initialization, auxiliary regularization, and new-instance discovery during propagation. We will refine the wording to avoid overstatement and make this positioning clearer. Training schedule (R2-Q5): The 1000 epochs refer to the maximum training budget. During training, we apply random augmentations to the original image as validation images and evaluate validation AUC every 10 epochs; early stopping is triggered if the AUC does not improve for 5 consecutive evaluation steps. In practice, early stopping usually terminates optimization before this limit. Thus, the training remains lightweight. Robustness analysis (R3): We agree that broader robustness analysis, including multi-dataset ablations, would further strengthen the conclusion. In accordance with the rebuttal guidelines, we cannot present additional ablation results here, but we will incorporate this suggestion in future work to better assess the robustness of each component.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviews are mixed: two weak accept and one weak reject. The work is practical with strong empirical results with fixable issues. Points to address add or justify instance-level metrics one-shot vs. baseline compare with EM-specific methods | The proposed method effectively adapts visual prompt tuning and SAM3 tracking to serial EM workflows. The final manuscript must temper instance segmentation and tracking claims unless additional metrics are added. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes POT-SAM3, a parameter-efficient one-shot adaptation strategy for serial-section electron microscopy segmentation. The method freezes SAM3 and learns a small set of concept prompt tokens from a single annotated section, then uses the learned tokens for automatic propagation across the remaining sections. The framework also includes auxiliary regularization and a new-instance discovery mechanism to handle propagation over serial EM data. The initial reviews were mixed but overall slightly positive, with scores of 4 / 3 / 4.Reviewers appreciated the practical motivation, the low-interaction EM annotation setting, the parameter-efficient design, and the reported empirical improvements over SAM2/3, PerSAM, HSNet, and nnU-Net baselines. The main concerns were limited comparison to EM-specific baselines, ambiguity in the “one-shot” framing, unclear details about the nnU-Net 10-shot comparison, lack of instance-level and tracking-level metrics despite the tracking/propagation framing, and limited robustness analysis across sequences and datasets. The rebuttal clarified several important points. The authors explained that all one-shot baselines use the same first annotated section, clarified the HSNet and nnU-Net(10) settings, positioned POT-SAM3 as a parameter-efficient low-interaction workflow rather than a new foundation model, and explained the intended first-section assumption. They also acknowledged that instance-level and tracking-level metrics would make the evaluation more complete, but did not provide new quantitative results, consistent with rebuttal constraints. Some limitations remain. The current evidence still relies mostly on Dice-style segmentation metrics, which may obscure instance-level and propagation-specific failures such as split/merge errors, identity inconsistency, false new-instance discovery, and track fragmentation. The comparison to EM-specific methods and the robustness analysis across datasets remain limited. These issues prevent the paper from being a strong accept. After rebuttal, the effective reviewer summary is A / R / A, treating the no-update reviewer as retaining the initial weak accept. Reviewer 1’s positive final opinion was based mainly on the clarified one-shot setting, the nnU-Net supervision budget, and the parameter-efficient framing. Reviewer 2 maintained reject, arguing that the remaining weaknesses were still substantial. Reviewer 3 did not update but initially leaned positive due to the practical workflow and substantial empirical gains. I recommend Accept. Although the paper has moderate novelty and incomplete instance/tracking-level evaluation, the problem is practically important, the workflow is well aligned with serial EM annotation, and the rebuttal clarified the main experimental-setting ambiguities. The remaining issues should be explicitly acknowledged in the final version, especially the lack of instance-level and tracking-level metrics, limited EM-specific baseline comparison, and limited robustness analysis. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers generally agreed that the paper addresses an important and practical problem in serial-section EM segmentation and presents a parameter-efficient adaptation of SAM3 that substantially reduces annotation and interaction requirements while achieving strong performance across multiple public datasets. The rebuttal successfully clarified concerns regarding the one-shot protocol, baseline comparisons, supervision budget, workflow assumptions, and training schedule, resolving several ambiguities raised during review. While concerns remain regarding the absence of instance-level and tracking-level metrics, limited robustness analysis, and moderate methodological novelty, these issues primarily affect evaluation completeness rather than the validity of the proposed approach or the strength of the reported empirical results. Given the consistent performance gains, practical significance, and generally positive reviewer assessments, I believe the strengths outweigh the remaining weaknesses and recommend acceptance.

title: Probe-EM: Targeted Neuron Tracing via Training-Free Semantic Verification
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The problem framing is well-motivated and aligned with practical proofreading workflows: targeted, seed-driven tracing is genuinely more useful than global pairwise merge classification when researchers want to follow specific neuronal populations rather than correct the entire volume. 2.The geometric prompt sampling design (anchor / probe / rear points) is principled. The ablation showing that removing GPS reduces F1 from 0.586 to 0.328 confirms that center-only prompting causes mask leakage, and the rear-point construction is a sensible safeguard against over-expansion. 3.The framework is integrated into Neuroglancer and evaluated with a human-in-the-loop study involving three annotators, which is uncommon in method-focused papers and provides useful evidence of practical utility.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Missing comparison against the most relevant SOTA. eg. RoboEM is cited but not included as a baseline. The paper should at minimum justify why RoboEM cannot be compared on the SCN data, ideally include it. Also SAM3 is actually developed to solve the continuity problem, but this paper only uses SAM2. 2.”Training-free” framing is overstated. DASV depends on NeuroSAM 2, which is fine-tuned on the EMNeuron dataset. The method is training-free with respect to connectivity supervision but not with respect to neuronal EM imagery. The abstract and contributions should distinguish these clearly, otherwise the comparison against learning-based baselines (which only see SCN training labels) is not fully fair. 3.The evaluation should be more comprehensive. Only one dataset (SCN) is used, with 24 axon fascicles and 8 soma-containing neurons in the test set. Soma-seeded tracing in particular is evaluated on a very small sample. No standard deviations or per-neuron variance are reported, and no statistical tests support the comparisons in Table 1. 4.What fraction of HSS-pruned branches were actually correct (false positives of the topological pruning)? When does ASP propagation drift? The paper would benefit from a qualitative discussion of where the method breaks. 5.Skeleton-node-based recall/precision/F1 is reasonable but does not align with metrics commonly used in connectomics benchmarking such as expected run length (ERL), split rate, and merge rate. Without these, the results are not directly comparable to the broader literature on EM segmentation correction. Also the hyperparameter robustness is not analyzed. δ = 500 nm, τ_high = 0.5, τ_low = 0.1, τ_occ = 0.6, K = 5, N = 5, and the topological pruning thresholds are all fixed empirically. Only N is partially ablated. Cross-dataset generalization, which is one of the main motivations for going training-free, is not evaluated. 6.Minor: Equation (1) introduces ε_s without explicitly defining it as the terminal endpoint set (this is only clear from context), and the symbol for the search radius (δ) collides with the distance threshold notation used elsewhere in the literature.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Overall idea is elegant, in EM segmentation, it’s typically more difficult to predict correct continuity through thin neurite instances than to verify if two splits belong to the same neuron. The authors successfully taps into that observation and strategically combined a simple prober with a powerful verification engine to address this limitation. The train-free paradigm is notably gonna be a lot more transferable to new datasets and new problems easier and is highly practical. Fully exploited the capabilities of SAM2, could provide useful data point for the industry on how to utilizes ever improving foundation models.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: I initially expected the prober to be more intelligent, e.g. using some sort of direction / local shape priors to get some initial confidence score but it seems quite basic, just taking everything within a distance notably the method still requires a human annotator in the loop, but didn’t go one step further to try to automate this step as well, I’d be curious what the benchmark looks like (e.g. in table 2, a “automated annotator” group with much lower time but likely lower F1 score)
reviewer_2_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviewer_3_strengths: Practical and training-free framework. A key strength of the paper is the proposal of a method that does not require task-specific training. By leveraging a pretrained foundation model within a geometric tracing framework, Probe-EM can be directly deployed, which is highly appealing in connectomics workflows where annotation and training data are expensive to obtain. Integration into an interactive tool. The integration with Neuroglancer significantly enhances the practical relevance of the work. Providing an interactive proofreading tool increases the potential impact of the method for real-world annotation pipelines and user-assisted reconstruction tasks. Strong empirical performance under the presented setup. Under the experimental conditions described, Probe-EM outperforms several learning-based baselines. This is particularly noteworthy given that the competing methods require training, whereas the proposed approach does not. Ablation study supporting method design. The paper includes a detailed ablation study analyzing the contribution of key components (Planar Ensemble Consensus, Axial Spatio-Temporal Propagation, and Geometric Point Sampling). The results show clear performance degradation when these components are removed, supporting the design choices, with ASP appearing particularly critical. User study demonstrating practical benefits. The evaluation with multiple annotators shows improvements in annotation speed while maintaining or improving segmentation quality. This is an important aspect for connectomics applications, where manual proofreading is a major bottleneck. Use of public data and potential reproducibility. The experiments are conducted on a subset of a public dataset (SCN), which facilitates reproducibility. The authors also state that code and data will be released, which, if fulfilled, would further strengthen the contribution.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Insufficient description of the foundation model (NeuroSAM 2). The proposed method critically depends on the pretrained model used for semantic verification. However, NeuroSAM 2 is not described in sufficient detail. It is unclear how this model was obtained (e.g., architecture, training data, fine-tuning procedure), and it does not appear to be publicly available. Moreover, despite being listed as a main contribution (together with the dimension-aware semantic verification module), its role and implementation are not adequately explained. This limits the interpretability and reproducibility of the approach. Limited transparency of the experimental setup. While the SCN dataset is described, the specific subset used for training and evaluation is not sufficiently detailed. The manuscript mentions the use of patches from a limited number of axon fascicles and soma-containing neurons, but does not report the total number of samples, patch size, etc. These details are important for assessing the robustness and generalizability of the results. Incomplete description of baseline training protocols. The training setup for the learning-based baselines lacks important details (e.g., learning rate scheduling, validation strategy, data augmentation, convergence behavior). Given that Probe-EM is compared against these methods, it is important to ensure that the baselines are properly optimized. Providing a more detailed description (e.g., in a supplementary table) would strengthen the validity of the comparison. Limited analysis of precision–recall trade-offs. The reported results show noticeable imbalances between precision and recall in several cases. However, the paper does not provide sufficient analysis or discussion of these trade-offs. A deeper examination of failure modes (e.g., over-segmentation vs under-segmentation) would help better understand the behavior of the method and its practical implications.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the Meta-Reviewer (MR) and reviewers (R1, R2, R3) for their constructive feedback and address the major concerns below: 1.”Training-Free” Formulation & NeuroSAM 2 Details (MR, R1, R3) We will refine “training-free” to “zero-shot connectivity inference” to avoid ambiguity. NeuroSAM 2 adapts SAM 2 by fine-tuning the prompt encoder and mask decoder (frozen image encoder) on EMNeuron to learn generalizable EM features. This utilizes Focal/Dice/IoU losses (25k iters, AdamW, batch=16, lr=1e-5, decay=4e-5). Model weights will be open-sourced. 2.Evaluation Comprehensiveness (MR, R1) Zero-Shot Generalization: Evaluated directly on the H01 dataset (6 test neurons, soma-based tracing), Probe-EM achieved Precision=0.447, Recall=0.556, and F1=0.450 without retraining, demonstrating robust cross-dataset transferability. Variance & Significance: Our per-neuron F1 for soma-seeded tracing is 0.544 ± 0.202, demonstrating higher accuracy and stability than the top baseline (0.293 ± 0.320) with statistical significance (p=0.011, paired t-test). Throughput: As total tracing time fluctuates with morphological complexity, we report operational throughput on a single RTX 4090: on average, it takes ~0.19s to search for a candidate pair and ~1.89s to infer its connectivity. 3.Missing Baselines & Metrics (MR, R1) RoboEM: While RoboEM is a pioneering method, fundamental design differences preclude a direct comparison. First, paradigms differ: RoboEM extracts skeletons directly from raw EM images, making it sensitive to local alignment offsets and requiring high spatial continuity. Conversely, Probe-EM starts from segmentation results, utilizing an exploratory single-seed search to connect over-segmented blocks. Second, architectural focuses diverge: RoboEM targets the connectivity of axons and dendritic spines, whereas Probe-EM focuses on reconstructing connections involving axons and complex soma regions. Regarding ERL: Evaluated on the Axon Fascicle Tracing task, Probe-EM achieves an ERL of 222.46 µm, outperforming the top baseline (157.86 µm). SAM 3: We fine-tuned SAM 2 as SAM 3’s Promptable Concept Segmentation (PCS) introduces a language modality unnecessary for our geometry-driven tracing, while SAM 2’s memory already effectively handles cross-slice continuity. Evaluating SAM 3 and exploring language-guided connectomics will be discussed as future work. 4.”Automated Annotator” Benchmark (R2) Table 1 already serves as the fully automated baseline (zero manual time). Its naturally lower F1 score compared to the human-assisted workflow (Table 2) highlights why human-in-the-loop proofreading remains essential to achieve the near-perfect fidelity required in connectomics. 5.Failure Modes & PR Trade-offs (R1, R3) Failure Modes: Across 32 test neurons, HSS pruned 5 complex candidates, mistakenly discarding only one true segment. For ASP, increasing window N from 5 to 8 degrades F1 (Table 3) as cumulative tracking errors cause mask drift into parallel structures. Future work will explore trajectory-guided memory constraints to mitigate these errors. PR Trade-offs: The Recall > Precision imbalance deliberately targets human-in-the-loop workflows. Rejecting false proposals takes seconds, whereas manually searching in PB-scale volumes demands massive labor. Conversely, supervised baselines typically miss rare connections, sacrificing Recall for Precision. 6.HSS Search Strategy (R2) HSS adopts a “lenient-in, strict-out” strategy: all nearby segments are included regardless of morphology to ensure high recall, while the DASV module subsequently ensures precision through rigorous filtering. 7.Experimental Details (R3) As per Sec. 3.2, baselines were trained on 433 positive/8,699 negative pairs. Input patches of 120x120x30 were centered at contact interfaces. Optimization: 50 epochs (converged), Adam (lr=1e-4), spatial augmentations, and WeightedRandomSampler. Models were selected via max validation F1 (80/20 split).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): There are discrepancies among the three reviewers, consisting of strong accept, weak accept, and weak reject. The paper tackles the important problem of neuron tracing in EM volumes, in which a raining-free method is proposed to probe-then-verify the plausible merges, with favorable empirical results. Meanwhile, there are a number of aspects of the work that raise concerns. It would be beneficial if the authors provide further input and clarifications in the areas specifically brought out by the reviewers, including but not limited to, insufficient details of NeuroSAM 2 (an important ingredient of the proposed method), insufficient details of empirical setup, empirical evaluation on limited datasets, limited comparison baselines, and concerns of overstated claims. | Most of the concerns have been addressed by the rebuttal. That said, there remain concerns such as empirical comparison with RoboEM. The authors are encouraged to carefully follow the reviews and revise the draft accordingly, if it is eventually accepted by this round of MICCAI. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The decision is to accept the paper. During the rebuttal phase, the authors effectively addressed critical reviewer concerns by clarifying foundation model details, providing cross dataset generalization results, and reporting additional evaluation metrics. Although opinions were initially mixed regarding methodological transparency, the thorough clarifications and the clear utility of the interactive proofreading tool confirm that this work is a valuable contribution to the community. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend acceptance for this paper. I think the problem is meaningful and the approach is reasonable. In particular, the probing–verification cycle is interesting. The use of foundation models is also appreciated and appears useful. Please make sure that the revised submission is within the 8-page limit. The current version is slightly over 8 pages, and I am not sure why it was not desk-rejected, as it appears to exceed the 8-page limitation policy.

title: Prototype-Driven Robust Domain Generalization in Corneal Endothelial Cell Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: S1.The paper addresses corneal endothelial cell segmentation, which is clinically relevant for diagnosis and monitoring. Moreover, it tackles the problem of domain generalization, which is pervasive in medical image computing, where datasets are often limited and models must remain robust to variations across centers, devices, and pathologies. S2.The proposed method demonstrates strong empirical performance across multiple domain shifts, including cross-center, cross-disease, cross-device, and cross-species scenarios. This is a comprehensive and meaningful evaluation of domain generalization. S3.The paper proposes a novel and non-trivial extension of (SGC) by introducing error prototypes to model difficult regions. The overall framework is modular and could, in principle, be adapted to other segmentation tasks or integrated into different architectures. S4.The method appears reasonably robust to hyper-parameters, as supported by the sensitive analysis. This supports the practical applicability of the method. S5.The use of an error-focused segmentation loss can be interpreted as a form of spatial hard-example mining, encouraging the model to focus on regions where previous predictions were incorrect. This is a simple and intuitive mechanism to improve performance on challenging areas.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: W1.I find the connection between the proposed method and its intended goal of domain generalization to be somewhat unclear. While the use of prototype-based approaches (such as SGC) is well motivated for few-shot learning, it is less clear how extending this framework with cell and error prototypes should improve robustness to domain shifts. The authors argue that prototypes guide segmentation through similarity matching and thereby “decouple feature recognition from domain-specific noise,” but it is not entirely clear how this decoupling is actually achieved in practice. In particular, the method does not appear to explicitly ensure that the cell prototypes capture domain-invariant features. Similarly, error prototypes, defined based on regions where the model fails during training, may not necessarily correspond to domain-dependent features. As a result, it remains unclear why cell prototypes should transfer across domains, or why error prototypes would consistently identify unreliable features in unseen settings, as the method does not appear to include explicit mechanisms that encourage this behavior. Overall, while the intuition behind separating “reliable” and “unreliable” regions is reasonable, the link between this design and improved domain generalization remains largely implicit and is not convincingly supported by the methodology. This raises the question of whether the proposed approach should be considered a domain generalization method, or rather a form of hard-example mining (thanks to the error-focused segmentation loss and the error prototypes) that incidentally improves performance on the CEC segmentation task. W2.Related to the previous point, a more detailed ablation study would be helpful to better understand what drives the observed performance gains, and in particular whether they stem from the incorporation of hard-example mining strategies. The current ablation appears relatively coarse, as multiple components are introduced simultaneously (e. g. , the prototype enhancer, ablated as a whole, combines contrastive learning and prototype refinement, while the prototype allocator introduces confidence maps and noise mitigation). This makes it difficult to attribute performance gains to specific design choices. More importantly, the contributions of the different loss terms are not fully disentangled. The optimized objective combines a standard segmentation loss, an error-focused (hard-mining) segmentation loss, and a contrastive loss, but their individual impact is not explicitly evaluated in isolation. In particular, it would be informative to assess how much of the improvement is due to the hard-mining component, and whether applying a similar strategy to baseline methods would yield comparable gains. W3.The experimental evaluation focuses primarily on cross-domain scenarios, but does not explicitly report performance on the training domain. It would be useful to assess how the proposed method performs in-domain, in order to better understand the trade-off between improving domain generalization and maintaining performance on the source distribution. Also, reporting in-domain performance would help better understand whether the observed improvements are specific to domain generalization, or instead reflect more general effects of the training strategy, such as the use of error-focused supervision. W4.The t-SNE visualizations provide a qualitative illustration of how the proposed method separates cell and error features, but provide limited evidence to support the domain generalization claims. First, since the method is explicitly designed to distinguish between cell and error prototypes, the observed separation between them may be expected and may not necessarily demonstrate improved generalization. Second, the plots do not provide insight into how features from different domains are distributed. In particular, samples are not stratified by domain, which makes it difficult to assess whether the proposed method effectively reduces the domain gap or aligns representations across domains. Using domain-specific color coding could provide better evidence of improved generalization. W5.[Minor] Section 2.3 indicates that the pool of prototypes is N=128.In Section 3.1, it is set to N=3.This could be clarified. Also, it would be helpful to specify whether N=3 refers to the total number of prototypes or to the number of prototypes per type (cell and error). W6.[Minor] The description of the prototype update mechanism in Section 2.3 is not completely clear. It would be helpful to clarify whether the update rule is applied in the same way to both cell and error prototypes. Additionally, it is not specified whether cell and error prototypes are treated as negative pairs in the contrastive learning loss, even when they are considered similar according to the similarity function. W7.[Minor] The method relies on an iterative procedure in which the predicted segmentation from the previous epoch is used to estimate error regions for the next epoch. It is not entirely clear how this process is initialized, particularly during the first epoch when no prior prediction is available.

reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Clinically motivated The domain generalization problem in CEC segmentation is real, important, and underexplored. The paper does an excellent job motivating why existing methods fail, they overfit to single-center, single-device training distributions, and Fig. 1 powerfully illustrates these failure modes with concrete Dice drop numbers. 2.Novel idea The prototype strategy is clever. Rather than only learning what cells look like (as standard prototypical networks do), ProtoCEC explicitly learns what segmentation failures look like via the Error Prototype Pool. This is an elegant and well-motivated design choice that distinguishes the work from prior art. 3.Comprehensive evaluation Testing across four distinct distribution shift scenarios; cross-center, cross-disease, cross-device, and cross-species; is a robust way to test different cases. 4.Consistent performance improvements The reported gains are consistent and meaningful: +3.2%, +4.5%, +7.7%, and +3.6% over the second-best method across the four scenarios. These are not marginal improvements.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Prototype collector There is some ambiguity in the paper regarding the Cell Prototype Pool and Error Prototype Pool, is it “derived from the predicted mask P” and the Error Prototype Pool is “extracted from the error mask M_ER”. However, it is never explicitly explained how the superpixel-guided clustering (SGC) extracts prototypes from these two sources in practice: Does SGC operate on the feature map masked by P, or on the full feature map with P as a soft weight? For the error branch, does the shared encoder process I_ER as a completely separate forward pass, or are features reused from the main forward pass? If it is a separate forward pass through the shared encoder, what is the computational cost during training? At epoch 1, there is no previous prediction — how is the cold start handled? The paper is completely silent on this 2.The prototype allocator’s standardization step Is very aggressive When scell > serror, the paper completely replaces the pixel feature f with its nearest cell prototype: f’ = arg max sim(f, p) p ∈ Pcell This is a hard replacement, the original feature is discarded entirely. This raises serious concerns: Fine-grained spatial details present in f but not captured by any prototype are permanently lost With only 128 prototypes per pool, can the library truly represent all valid cell morphologies across cross-species scenarios? No ablation compares hard replacement vs soft blending (e.g., f’ = α × nearest_proto + (1-α) × f) I would suggest test the algorithm with soft blending if possible 3.The bottleneck features are never guided The PA module only operates on skip connections at Block 2, 3, and 4.The deepest bottleneck features flow directly to the decoder without any prototype guidance: Encoder bottleneck → Decoder (unguided, potentially domain-noisy) Block 2,3,4 skip → PA → Decoder (guided and cleaned) The bottleneck arguably contains the most semantically rich and domain-sensitive features. Is there any reason that the authors decided to avoid that in the bottleneck layer, that’s need to be added in the Ablation studies section 4.Hyperparameter justifications are weak Several key hyperparameters are fixed without adequate justification: τ (temperature) 0.1 No sensitivity analysis provided η (momentum) 0.9 No sensitivity analysis Dual thresholds 0.3 / 0.8 No ablation on these critical values K per level 128 for all same capacity for all encoder levels seems suboptimal 5.SIM needs more Justification The Structural Importance Mapping function is directly borrowed from a reference. The paper doesn’t justify why SIM specifically is the right choice over simpler alternatives such as Gaussian blur of the error mask No ablation compares SIM against these simpler alternatives, making it unclear whether the SDF-based exponential formulation is truly necessary. 6.Dataset sizes are concerning for generalization claims The external test sets are quite small: Cross-device (Rodrep): 52 images ← very small! Cross-species (Alisarine): 30 images ← extremely small! With only 30 images for the cross-species evaluation, the +3.6% improvement over the second-best method may not be statistically reliable. No statistical significance testing (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank test) is reported for any of the comparisons. 7.Lack of related work The paper claims ProtoCEC is “the first prototype-driven framework tailored for corneal endothelial cell segmentation”, but this claim is not carefully scoped. Prototype learning has been extensively applied in medical image segmentation more broadly. The authors should either: More carefully scope this claim to CEC segmentation specifically, or provide a proper related work section discussing prototype-based methods in medical imaging. Notably, there is no related work section at all. Minor Comments What does robust mean in the title ?, I recommend to remove that word Fig. 2 is very dense and difficult to read and understand The conclusion is very brief and adds little beyond what is already in the abstract

reviewer_3_strengths: 1) The concept of explicitly mining and utilizing “error prototypes” alongside valid cell prototypes is innovative. By actively learning the feature signatures of typical failure modes and using them to suppress domain-specific artifacts via the Prototype Allocator, the authors provide a structurally elegant solution to domain shift. 2) The evaluation design is strong. Testing the framework against four distinct out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios (cross-center, cross-disease, cross-device, and cross-species) directly addresses the clinical reality of heterogeneous data and shows the model’s versatility. 3) ProtoCEC demonstrates clear, significant margins over a wide array of recent state-of-the-art baselines (+3.2% to +7.7% Dice improvements across OOD sets). 4) The paper provides a convincing ablation study that isolates the contributions of individual modules (PC, PE, PA) and maps the model’s sensitivity to key hyperparameters, demonstrating that the architectural choices are justified and not arbitrary. 5) The method is not limited to the proposed application and can be extended and adapted to other segmentation tasks.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) While the OOD evaluation is extensive, the paper lacks detail on how the ground truth annotations were obtained for the four external target datasets (DATA-I, DATA-II, Rodrep, Alisarine). It is critical to clarify whether these were annotated by the same clinical experts as the source dataset, as varying annotation standards across datasets could introduce bias into the cross-domain evaluation. 2) The source dataset (CED) and the primary target datasets (DATA-I, DATA-II) appear to be private/in-house. The manuscript does not state whether the code, pre-trained models, or datasets will be made publicly available upon publication. Given the complex nature of the training pipeline, releasing the code is highly recommended. 3) The authors claim the inference is “streamlined for real-time application”, but no metrics (e.g., inference time per image) are provided to substantiate this claim or compare the computational overhead against the baseline U-Net/ResNet models. 4) The authors should clarify if dice score is computed over the boundary overlap or over cell area? 5) How does this pipeline compare against methods that use foundation models in their pipeline, such as Cellpose SAM?
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: 1.Domain Generalization (R1, R2) While the clinical motivation and evaluation of this work are anchored in CCM, our architectural innovations constitute a targeted domain generalization strategy. Rather than relying on standard hard-example mining that incidentally improves segmentation, our framework explicitly models and mitigates domain gaps across distinct scenarios (cross-center/disease/device/species). However, we agree with the reviewer that our claims should be precisely scoped, and will revise our tone, framing ProtoCEC primarily as a robust framework tailored for CCM. In practice, this robustness is achieved because the decoder never processes raw, domain-specific features. The Prototype Allocator acts as a structural adapter: it strictly standardizes valid features by mapping them to purified canonical prototypes, while utilizing error prototypes to actively attenuate OOD noise. 2.Cross-Domain Alignment & t-SNE (R1) Beyond 2D visual projections, we rely on quantitative alignment evidence: tracking allocated features from the four unseen domains revealed that 117 of 128 cell prototype clusters embed mixed-domain features (initially omitted for space). This proves cross-domain alignment. Furthermore, separating cell and error prototypes in Fig. 5 is not merely a loss artifact; trapping deceptive OOD patterns drives our robustness. 3.In-Domain Performance (R1) Error-focused supervision provides a general uplift without sacrificing source Dice. On the held-out source test set (omitted for space), ProtoCEC achieved 0.858 Dice, outperforming SOTA (SPG-Net) by 4.4%, proving standardization suppresses noise while enhancing refinement. 4.Hard-Mining vs. Standardization (R1) While hard-example mining strengthens intra-domain boundaries, our framework goes further by projecting unseen domain features onto a stable, discrete manifold. Decoupling loss alone without other components (L_seg: 0.688, L_error: 0.705, L_con: 0.730) confirms standardization overwrites domain-sensitive textures with invariant geometric configurations (e.g., SGC-captured repetitive hexagonal structures). This yields a 2.5% OOD gain over L_error (3.3% when applied to SPG-Net), demonstrating that it drives optimal OOD generalization across all shift scenarios, rather than merely performing hard mining. 5.Module Designs, Aggressiveness & Scope (R1, R2) SGC operates strictly on hard-masked regions (binarized P and M_ER) without soft weights. Processing the error image via a separate pass doubles training computation but adds zero inference overhead. A 30-epoch warm-up reliably prepares robust initial prototypes (apologies, omitted). To filter domain interference, hard replacement overwrites noise for optimal OOD generalization (0.765 Avg. Dice) vs. soft blending at α=0.5 (0.742). Fine details are preserved via unguided bottleneck/decoder pathways. Guiding the deepest bottleneck causes over-regularization (0.749) vs. skip connections only (0.765). Parameters (τ=0.1, η=0.9, thresholds 0.3/0.8, pool capacity K=128, image-specific per-class prototypes N=3) were optimized via grid search. SIM uses an SDF-based exponential formulation, assigning unit weights inside and smoothly decaying outside to enhance boundary contrast. Wilcoxon tests confirm significant gains across all OOD sets (p<0.001). We will revise the “first” claim. Sub-component analysis: PE (contrastive only 0.730, +update 0.735) and PA (suppression only 0.738, +confidence 0.748). 6.Annotation, Speed & Foundation Models (R3) External annotations (DATA-I/II) share the exact CED source pipeline, cross-verified by three experts. Rodrep and Alisarine are public. Code will be open-sourced; ProtoCEC achieves real-time inference (20ms/image, RTX 3090), faster than SPG-Net (25ms). Dice is computed over boundary overlap, which is critical for CEC morphometry. ProtoCEC (0.765) outperforms Cellpose (0.732) and SAM (0.678) on OOD sets, as generic models lack structural priors for low-contrast CECs.

title: R2P-SAM: Root-to-Prompt Hair Instance Segmentation with Geometric Priors under Point Supervision
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that R2P-SAM achieves superior instance separation and boundary accuracy under dense overlap. 2.Casting instance segmentation as a Root-to-Prompt generation task is conceptually clean and well-motivated. It aligns naturally with SAM’s prompting paradigm and avoids heavy redesign.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The method highly relies on pretrained model like SAM, which is unfair when compared with methods in the point-supervision setting. 2.The method is not compared against intuitive cascade methods. For example, if we train a detector (such as YOLO, FCOS, DETR, using a fixed box size if necessary), and use the detected box centers as the point prompts for SAM, what accuracy can be achieved? 3.Based on the visualization, oriented object detection seems to be very suitable for hairs. It would be interesting to see if oriented boxes could be helpful in the task setting. [1] Wholly-WOOD: Wholly Leveraging Diversified-quality Labels for Weakly-supervised Oriented Object Detection [2] Point2RBox-v2: Rethinking Point-supervised Oriented Object Detection with Spatial Layout Among Instances

reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The idea of transforming sparse root signals into coherent, skeleton-aligned prompt trajectories is well motivated and technically interesting. 2.The paper is clearly written and generally easy to follow. 3.Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.R2P-SAM mainly samples a series of positive points as prompts for SAM-based segmentation. Have the authors considered incorporating additional prompt types, such as negative points or bounding boxes? It would be interesting to investigate whether these supplementary prompts could further improve segmentation performance. 2.In the PGR stage, the method applies SAM to cropped image regions rather than to the full image. While cropping may improve segmentation granularity, it also increases inference cost and may make the comparison less fair when baseline methods do not use the same strategy. It would therefore be helpful for the authors to report the performance of the method without cropping. In addition, an ablation that removes PGR and directly applies coarse point prompts together with cropping would further clarify the contribution of the proposed design. 3.Table 1 is currently not presented in a very polished format. I would recommend revising it using a standard three-line table style, consistent with the presentation of Tables 2 and 3.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The problem formulation is sensible. Hair roots are spatially non-overlapping and clinically meaningful, so using them as anchor points for prompting SAM is a natural fit for this application. The root-to-prompt framing is a reasonable way to bridge the gap between sparse annotations and instance-level masks. The geometric prior calibration with three complementary fields is technically well thought out. The tangent field provides directional flow along the strand, the feasible region constrains where prompts can land, and the consistency field dampens updates at junctions where strand crossings create ambiguity. The ablation in Table 3 confirms that each component contributes meaningfully. The pixel-wise max heatmap generation instead of summation is a small but useful design choice. The intensity profile comparison in Fig. 3(d) clearly shows that summation merges adjacent roots while maximization preserves distinct peaks, which matters for dense strand regions. The qualitative results in Fig. 5 are convincing, especially on the Long-Hair dataset where overlapping strands are a real challenge. The method maintains strand continuity better than the baselines.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: One of the three evaluation datasets (Long-Hair) is private. This is a significant reproducibility concern, especially since it is the most challenging dataset in the paper and the one where the method shows the largest improvements. Without access to this data, the main results cannot be independently verified. All baselines are general purpose weakly supervised methods (DiscoBox, BoxLevelset, Box2Mask, SAPNet, P2Seg, PointSup) that were not designed for thin curvilinear structures. There is no comparison with methods specifically tailored for elongated objects like vessels or fibers, and no fully supervised upper bound is reported. Without knowing how far the results are from full supervision, it is hard to judge how well the method actually performs. The absolute performance numbers are still quite low. The best AP50 is 46.9% on Long-Hair and 50.0% on FDU. AP75 is around 23-31% across datasets. These numbers suggest the method is making progress but is far from being reliable enough for the clinical applications mentioned in the introduction. The paper claims clinical applicability for trichological analysis, but there is no validation with actual clinical metrics like hair density estimation, shaft diameter measurement, or terminal-to-vellus ratio computation. A downstream evaluation showing that the segmentations are good enough to extract clinically meaningful measurements would have strengthened the contribution. The geometric prior fields are derived from SAM’s pseudo-masks, which means the quality of the calibration is bounded by how good SAM’s initial coarse segmentation is. If SAM produces poor pseudo-masks for certain strand configurations, the geometric fields would also be unreliable. This dependency is not analyzed in the paper.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers and address questions below: Reviewer 1 W1 (Fairness): Weakly supervised fairness relies on annotation cost, not backbone size. Using frozen models as infrastructure is a standard paradigm. Due to severe domain shifts, SAM’s pre-training advantage is marginal. Table 1 shows zero-shot SAM performs poorly, indicating our gain stems mainly from our root-to-prompt and geometric calibration design, not just SAM. W2 (Detector cascades): The suggested “fixed box size” fails for curvilinear hairs. Geometric box centers often hit background or intersecting strands, cascading misdetections to SAM. Moreover, detectors merely replace root localization, yielding isolated endpoints. Lacking centerline trajectories, they fail on overlaps (Fig. 1c). R2P-SAM solves this via learned topological priors instead of geometric centers. W3 (Oriented boxes): While oriented boxes seem intuitive, they require higher annotation cost than point supervision. Rigid rectangles cannot fit curvilinear topologies, causing angle ambiguity and encompassing neighboring strands. Learning morphology directly via point features is more natural. We will explore oriented boxes in future work. Reviewer 2 W1 (Negative prompts): Bounding boxes violate point supervision, increase annotation costs, and suffer geometric ambiguity on crossing structures (Table 1). Furthermore, automatically defining reliable negative points without dense masks is challenging and introduces noise. Instead, our PriorNet provides implicit negative guidance by suppressing negative roots via Eq. 2.W2 (Cropping): The requested ablation (cropping without PGR) aligns with Table 3’s first row, yielding 0.188 AP75.Full PGR improves this to 0.235, proving geometric calibration, not cropping alone, drives the gain. Second, adapting SAM to high-res images causes severe scale mismatch for thin hairs and prohibitive VRAM limits. Processing uncropped full images squeezes strands into sub-pixel features, causing SAM to fail. Thus, cropping is a mandatory engineering step. We will detail no-cropping baselines in the final version. W3 (Formatting): We will revise Table 1 into a standard three-line format. Reviewer 3 W1 (Reproducibility): To facilitate future research, we will open-source our annotated instance test sets (long/short hair) and the complete R2P-SAM codebase in the final version. W2 (Upper bounds & Baselines): Public hair datasets lack instance masks. We manually annotated test sets for reliable evaluation. Since training set annotation requires drastically more effort, we only created point labels, precluding fully supervised bounds (e.g., Mask R-CNN). Regarding specialized baselines, most vessel/fiber methods target fully supervised or semantic segmentation, misaligned with our weakly supervised instance setting. As dense annotation requires months of expert labor, we will complete and release full masks for upper bounds in future work. W3 & W4 (AP & Clinical): Low AP partly reflects a known mismatch between COCO IoU and 1-pixel thin structures. A 1-2 pixel shift drastically drops IoU despite visually correct topology. As Fig. 5 illustrates, R2P-SAM preserves strand continuity compared with baselines. Moreover, accurate instance-level separation of entangled hairs is a prerequisite for reliable trichological analysis. By mitigating strand merging, R2P-SAM enables downstream measurements (e.g., density, shaft width), which we will explore in future work. W5 (Pseudo-masks): We mitigated this via a quality-aware weight q (Eq. 2) based on geometric consistency, down-weighting losses for unreliable pseudo-masks. Table 3 confirms this: our baseline yields 0.188 AP75, while full PGR reaches 0.235.This proves our framework actively calibrates unreliable masks rather than being bounded by them. In extreme blur/entanglement where SAM fails completely, prior derivation is constrained. We will discuss failure modes in the conclusion of the final version.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers acknowledge a clean, application-targeted SAM adaptation with a well-motivated two-stage design and consistent gains across three trichoscopy datasets. Two are weakly positive overall, while one is moderately negative on grounds of reproducibility (the most challenging dataset is private), limited baseline scope (no thin-curvilinear-specialist comparison, no fully-supervised upper bound), and unsupported clinical-applicability claims. The split warrants a rebuttal phase. For the rebuttal, the most pressing items are the cascade-baseline experiment to isolate the contribution beyond a generic detector→SAM pipeline, and reproducibility steps for the private Long-Hair dataset. Further items raised by the reviewers — including a no-cropping ablation, a fully-supervised Mask R-CNN upper bound, and a discussion of SAM-pseudo-mask failure modes — should also be addressed. | The paper presents R2P-SAM, a coarse-to-fine pipeline for generating robust point prompts to drive a frozen SAM backbone for hair-strand instance segmentation, combining Rootness Probability Field learning with Geometric Prior-Guided Calibration. The root-to-prompt formulation is conceptually clean, well aligned with SAM’s prompting paradigm, and supported by extensive experiments across multiple datasets. After the rebuttal phase, two reviewers recommend acceptance, while R3 maintains a reject on the grounds of the private dataset, the absence of a fully supervised upper bound, low absolute performance, and unvalidated clinical claims. In my view, the conceptual strength of the root-to-prompt formulation and the breadth of the empirical evaluation merit acceptance on balance. That said, I share R3’s reproducibility concern, and would add that the manuscript lacks sufficient mathematical specification of the loss functions and the Geometric Prior Fields, which limits reproducibility independently of dataset access. I strongly urge the authors to revise the manuscript to clarify these points, and to release the code and dataset as committed in the rebuttal. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The authors provided additional clarifications, yet there are still some concerns about fully-supervised results and robustness / generalizability analysis such as evaluation on public datasets. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper develops a root-to-prompt mechanism tailored to thin, overlapping hair strands, with geometric fields for feasible regions, tangent direction, and consistency at strand junctions. The camera-ready should substantially temper the claims. The clinical applicability claims are not yet supported by downstream hair-analysis metrics such as hair density, shaft diameter, or terminal-to-vellus ratio.

title: ReDIVE: A Two-Stage Hybrid Network for Keratitis Diagnosis via Retinex-based Enhancement and Depth-Informed Vertical Embedding
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The motivation is clear and clinically meaningful. Integrating depth information into sequence-level infectious keratitis classification is a novel and promising idea. 2.The design of depth embedding and the strategy of treating frame-level features as distinct tokens provide valuable insights for sequence-based medical image analysis.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.As a core contribution, the CDMSR module lacks clear details: the computation of loss L_S1 (including L_tv and L_ent) and its design rationale are not explained. The definition of I_in is ambiguous; if it denotes the raw input, the normalized L1 loss between I’_raw and I_in may conflict with the goal of image enhancement. 2.The implementation is not well aligned with the core idea of depth-aware learning. It would be more reasonable to jointly optimize image feature encoding (Stage 2) and sequence classification (Stage 3), rather than using separate stages. The paper does not clarify whether every frame in the IVCM sequence is diagnostically informative; single-frame optimization may learn misleading features if some frames are non-informative. 3.The fairness of comparison is questionable: it is unclear whether baseline methods use single-frame or sequence inputs. The strong performance of the “w/o CDMSR & D_rel & D_abs” variant raises concerns that gains may come mainly from larger model parameters.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The proposed framework is logically organized. The CDMSR module addresses a real imaging problem in IVCM, namely low contrast and non-uniform illumination. The hybrid feature embedding then combines local image features with absolute and relative depth information, and the transformer models inter-frame dependencies for sequence classification. These components are conceptually aligned with the stated clinical and technical goals. The framework diagram is also clear and helpful. In addition, the statistical analysis of depth distributions across pathogen categories is valuable, since it provides empirical support for the proposed depth-informed design rather than relying only on intuition. The reported Kruskal–Wallis and Mann–Whitney test results strengthen the paper’s core claim.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper provides a fair amount of training detail, but given the complexity of the full pipeline, reproducibility remains a concern. The reported dataset is large and clinically meaningful, which is a strength, but the evaluation is still confined to a single-center in-house collection. The authors themselves acknowledge this limitation in the conclusion. Because the method makes strong claims about establishing a new paradigm for IVCM-based diagnosis, broader validation would be desirable.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The proposed methodology is well motivated. The idea of aggregating information across images in a sequence is important for classifying IVCM images since sequences will show complementary information from the same disease. Similarly, depth context can help with differentiating between variability in anatomy versus disease. Their model achieves remarkably high accuracy and AUC, outperforming several baselines.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: While the number of images in the dataset is high, the actual number of scans is relatively limited; the test set only has 3-4 patients in each category. While each patient has many images, these images will be correlated as they will show overlapping or adjacent anatomy and the same disease. Having so few patients may not represent the variability of disease presentation. Also, reporting the number of frames is somewhat deceptive as the proposed algorithm aggregates information across each sequence, so the number of sequences would be a better representation of the data. While the authors put a lot of emphasis on their image enhancement method and the depth context, they have relatively little impact on the results. The ablation study shows that without these, the AUC is still high (0.9924) and adding in CDMSR and Drel actually result in reduced AUC (0.9905). While the model with all components has the highest performance, the marginal differences and lack of statistical testing or measure of variation call into question whether this difference is meaningful. Most of the benefit in this study seems to be from aggregating images in a sequence. As mentioned above, the image enhancement and depth context have marginal impact on results, so the only apparent difference between the proposed method and the baseline ConvNeXT is the ViT to aggregate over the sequence. While this procedure does show superior results, the baseline methods all seem to be operating on each image independently, so they aren’t performing the same task. In order to truly evaluate the proposed algorithm, the baselines should perform a similar aggregation. Otherwise, they are mainly demonstrating that looking at a full sequence is better that evaluating from a single image.
